It is called "most severe" because its heat is the greatest among all hells. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the Dharma, one should endure all hardships": this means that for the sake of the Mahāyāna Dharma, one should endure cold, heat, hunger, thirst, wind, rain, knives, staves, and all other such sufferings. One must never abandon the Mahāyāna. If one abandons the Mahāyāna, one will fall into the Avīci hell and suffer immeasurable pain. Therefore, one should always uphold the Mahāyāna and never abandon it. This concludes the section on the gravity of the sin of slandering the Dharma. Next, the section on the gravity of the sin of slandering the Sangha: [The verse continues: "If one slanders the Sangha, the sin is even heavier; The suffering of the Avīci hell is most severe. For the sake of the Sangha, one should endure all hardships; One must never abandon the Mahāyāna. Question: Why is it said that the sin of slandering the Sangha is even heavier than the sin of slandering the Dharma? Answer: Because the Sangha is the field of merit. If one slanders the Sangha, one cuts off the source of blessings for all sentient beings. Furthermore, the Sangha maintains the Dharma and the sūtras. If one slanders the Sangha, it is as if one slanders the Dharma and the sūtras. Moreover, the Sangha is the vessel for the Dharma. If one slanders the Sangha, the Dharma has no vessel and cannot be propagated. For these reasons, the sin of slandering the Sangha is even heavier than the sin of slandering the Dharma. Regarding the phrase "the suffering of the Avīci hell is most severe": the meaning is as explained previously. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the Sangha, one should endure all hardships": this means that for the sake of the Mahāyāna Sangha, one should endure cold, heat, hunger, thirst, wind, rain, knives, staves, and all other such sufferings. One must never abandon the Mahāyāna. If one abandons the Mahāyāna, one will fall into the Avīci hell and suffer immeasurable pain. Therefore, one should always uphold the Mahāyāna and never abandon it. This concludes the section on the gravity of the sin of slandering the Sangha. Next, the section on the gravity of the sin of slandering the Bodhisattva: [The verse continues: "If one slanders a Bodhisattva, the sin is even heavier; The suffering of the Avīci hell is most severe. For the sake of the Bodhisattva, one should endure all hardships; One must never abandon the Mahāyāna. Question: Why is it said that the sin of slandering a Bodhisattva is even heavier than the sin of slandering the Sangha? Answer: Because a Bodhisattva is the root of the Sangha. If one slanders a Bodhisattva, one cuts off the root of the Sangha. Furthermore, a Bodhisattva practices the Dharma and the sūtras. If one slanders a Bodhisattva, it is as if one slanders the Dharma and the sūtras. Moreover, a Bodhisattva is the leader of the Sangha. If one slanders a Bodhisattva, the Sangha has no leader and cannot proceed. For these reasons, the sin of slandering a Bodhisattva is even heavier than the sin of slandering the Sangha. Regarding the phrase "the suffering of the Avīci hell is most severe": the meaning is as explained previously. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the Bodhisattva, one should endure all hardships": this means that for the sake of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva, one should endure cold, heat, hunger, thirst, wind, rain, knives, staves, and all other such sufferings. One must never abandon the Mahāyāna. If one abandons the Mahāyāna, one will fall into the Avīci hell and suffer immeasurable pain. Therefore, one should always uphold the Mahāyāna and never abandon it. This concludes the section on the gravity of the sin of slandering the Bodhisattva. Next, the section on the gravity of the sin of slandering the precepts: [The verse continues: "If one slanders the precepts, the sin is even heavier; The suffering of the Avīci hell is most severe. For the sake of the precepts, one should endure all hardships; One must never abandon the Mahāyāna. Question: Why is it said that the sin of slandering the precepts is even heavier than the sin of slandering a Bodhisattva? Answer: Because the pre
How much more so, then, for one who reviles those who uphold the Lotus Sūtra? The meaning is the same. Furthermore, the *Sūtra of the Assembly of the Victorious Heavenly King* states:

"The sin of killing Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of a great trichiliocosm is still light; the sin of slandering this sūtra is greater than that, leading to eternal entry into hell with no time of release.
It is the same for those who revile its reading and recitation. Now, it should further be said: [as follows].

How much more so for one who slanders those who uphold the Lotus Sutra? If these words did not exist, although one might know that the sutra contains statements of unique manifestation, one would not yet have understood the sutra’s intent regarding its transcendence.
Furthermore, it says that slandering the Buddha does not harm the two benefits [of self and others], whereas slandering others has the opposite effect.
It also says that the Buddha is without hatred or attachment; that slandering the Buddha is difficult; and that when the Buddha was in the world, sentient beings...

The masters such as Gen-shō and others now maintain that this principle applies to both cases; however, neither yet captures the intended meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Furthermore, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* states:
"The transgression of disparaging one who has generated the bodhicitta exceeds the five ānantarya sins, for those five ānantarya crimes do not involve the disparagement of all Buddha-dharmas.
To disparage one who has generated the bodhicitta is to destroy all Buddha-dharmas. Now, it should be said: [that this is the case].
Citing the *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*, [the text] asks:
"From 'Why is this so? to 'What is the principle of the three types of awakening (*trividhabodhi*)?'—what is the underlying logic? The answer states:
"Because this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the most profound and esoteric, it was not entrusted to Ānanda; rather, it was entrusted solely to Bhaisajyarāja and others because it is supremely secret."
Question: Since there are passages concerning the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) everywhere that teach and transform thousands of śrāvakas to enter it, why was this [text] alone not entrusted to Ānanda?
Why were the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Nirvāṇa* sūtras also not entrusted to him?
Why was it only this sūtra that Ānanda protected as the treasury of the Dharma in the past and will protect as the treasury of the Buddhas' Dharma in the future? Why is this so?
Is it because this sutra was not transmitted in this life that it is considered inferior to the dharmas of the past and future? Furthermore, it is said:
"Using poison as medicine is something a great physician can manage, but a minor master cannot. Now I ask: who is the great physician, and what is meant by "using poison as medicine"?
If this sutra is called "poison" because of its name "One Vehicle," then other sutras also contain the dharma of the One Vehicle.
Question: From the passage in the Sūtra beginning with “At that time, the World-Honored One” up until the verse concerning the honoring of those who uphold this sūtra—what is the meaning of this?

Answer: This clarifies that the merit of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (Lotus Sūtra) surpasses all others. Now, according to these passages, there are not just one or two instances throughout the preceding and following sections where it is stated that the *Lotus Sūtra* excels all other teachings.
If so, what is the purpose of citing works such as the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā* [to the contrary]?
In commenting upon and elucidating this wondrous sutra, one asks:
why does the prose preceding the verses at the beginning of the scripture state, "At that time, the Buddha again addressed [the assembly]... it is difficult to believe and difficult to understand"?

The answer is: it is stated directly that among the sutras of the three periods, this sutra is difficult to believe and understand, so as to cause [beings] to abandon the provisional and resort to the real.
Since birth is characterized by the principle of arising, which is profound, mysterious, and circuitous before it is realized, it is difficult to believe and understand.

Now, if one says that [the Buddha] causes [beings] to abandon the provisional and adhere to the real—just as in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, where all five hundred śrāvakas were rebuked, causing them all to abandon the provisional—and furthermore, in the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" of the *Avataṃsaka*, where [the assembly] was initially like the deaf and the mute, but later saw Mañjuśrī depart; [it follows that this too is a case of abandoning the provisional].
The *Bahudhātuka-sūtra* states: "If there are śrāvakas who are able to resolve their minds [for enlightenment], I shall likewise rejoice in them.

Is this not a passage concerning the relinquishing of the provisional and returning to the real? The *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* speaks of bestowing predictions of enlightenment upon śrāvakas during the second and third turnings;
is this not the same? In the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, it is said that all ten immortals entered the Real; as for calling this "detouring," this too is likewise [the case].
The *Adbhuta-dharma-paryāya* states: "One travels the great straight path without hindrance. Why, then, is the straight explained by means of the circuitous? Question:
The Sūtra says that Bhaiṣajyarāja comes and touches his head with his hand; what is the meaning of this? Answer: This clarifies that through the Dharma, a person becomes a teacher of supreme virtue.
There are seven such virtues: first, the Buddha’s robe covers him—the robe of gentleness and patience, endowed with shame and remorse.

Therefore, they are covered by the Buddha’s compassion; therefore, they are protected by the mindfulness of two Buddhas, because the Buddha skillfully protects and mindfully remembers those Bodhisattvas whose roots of virtue have matured;
thirdly, they possess great faith; fourthly, they possess great aspirations; fifthly, they possess roots of goodness;

sixthly, the Buddhas dwell together with them, sharing the chamber of loving-kindness and compassion and the dwelling of emptiness, wisdom, and the ultimate truth; seventhly, the Buddhas stroke their heads and teach them.

Because they are sustained by the Buddhas within their hearts, the current scriptural passage merely states that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who write, uphold, read, recite, and make offerings to [this sutra], as well as those who preach it, shall be "covered by robes" and even "touched by hands. This implies that one must write, uphold, read, and recite with the full fingers, being thus covered by the robes and so forth.
How then can it be said that they are "gentle and supple," etc.? If one were to say it refers to the Buddha’s robe—

Regarding those who are "gentle and so forth," how is it that they are called "Buddha-garments" and the like? After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, are all such individuals people who have regressed from the Mahāyāna and turned their minds [toward the Hīnayāna]?
Furthermore, at the beginning of the long prose section of the preceding part, it says that those seeking the Two Vehicles and those seeking to be Bodhisattvas all receive predictions;

do these also turn their minds [toward the Hīnayāna]? Are the eight classes of beings, such as devas and nāgas, also those who have regressed from the Mahāyāna and turned their minds [toward the Hīnayāna]?
Question: Regarding the passage from "Bhaiṣajyarāja" to "respectfully praised," what is its meaning? Answer: It clarifies that this is the *dharmakāya* relic which should be venerated.
First, it lists the five locations beginning with "If one speaks of"; next, from "Why is this so? onwards, it provides the explanation.
Furthermore, it was first revealed that these are whole-body śarīras, clarifying that both wisdom and principle are fully perfected, thereby possessing the complete Dharmakāya and Saṃbhogakāya.

From this, through reverse illumination, one is shown the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—passing through the stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering—thereby encompassing both bodhi and nirvāṇa, and exhausting both phenomenon and principle.

Now, [if one asks]: "Wisdom is practice; principle is teaching; perfection is the fruit. Why are there four?"* *(Note: The final sentence appears to be an incomplete rhetorical question or inquiry regarding the structure of the fourfold path or the relationship between the aforementioned categories.)*
The Dharma is gone, yet two remain; this second explanation further states that the four dharmas are fully complete.

Furthermore, how do these differ from the *Anantārthavyākaraṇa-sūtra* regarding their similarities and differences? Moreover, what distinguishes these four dharmas from the four dharmas of the various Mahāyāna traditions?

It is also said that when Buddhist images are fashioned or scriptures are transcribed, the *dharmakāya* and *śarīra* relics are enshrined within the image. [The Buddha] said: "All dharmas arise from causes; the Tathāgata..."
It is said that because those dharmas are extinguished through conditions, what the Great Śramaṇa has spoken of is the *dharmakāya-śarīra*.

Now, it is claimed that this was heard by Śāriputra as Ājñātakauṇḍinya recounted what the Buddha had taught; thus, the "three [teachings] regarding the *dharmakāya*" within the Four Noble Truths of the Hīnayāna refers to the *pañcāṅgika-dharmakāya* (the fivefold dharma-body) as a relic.
This citation serves as proof for the permanence [of the Buddha] in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

It is truly laughable that one would claim the śarīra of the Dharmakāya truly resides [within a stūpa]; how much more so when it is placed within clay and plaster, making that clay and plaster identical in meaning to the "five parts" (the structural components of a stūpa).

This is entirely unrelated to the text of this sūtra, for they differ in being Mahāyāna versus Hīnayāna, and in being general versus specific; they also differ in their provisional and ultimate applications.
Furthermore, it is asked: if one uses the analogy of inscribed verses to illustrate the scrolls of the sūtras, then the meaning of "that which is contained" is like entering a stūpa.
If one asks whether those who preach or read [this text] should also have a stūpa built for them, the meaning of the passage here is that a stūpa must be erected only in five specific cases.
Within the stūpa, there should already be the Dharma-body or the whole-body śarīra; if one refers to "solidified śarīra" under another name, this would be acceptable.
However, if one cites the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and claims that the names "Suchness" (*tathatā*) and "Wisdom of Suchness" (*tathatājñāna*) refer to the Dharma-body, then this is not so.
This [teaching] is the Dharma-body, not the śarīra-relics; herein it is simply stated that the teaching of the *Lotus Sūtra* is the śarīra-relic of the Dharma-body.
Therefore, where it says "in such places," these are precisely the locations of the śarīra. Who would say they reside in a person?
If the realized Dharma-body resides in a person, it resides within the body of Śākyamuni himself—why then must one specifically say it is in the *Lotus Sūtra*?

Question: From the section on Bhaiṣajyarāja up to the Bodhisattva path, what is the meaning? Answer: Because this is the direct cause, having already entered the count of kalpas, it is called "wholesome practice" (kuśala-caryā).
Now, if one enters the first asaṃkhyeya-kalpa of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, this is eternally unrelated to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Such a bodhisattva belongs precisely to the class who has neither heard nor understood [this sutra] until now; even after hearing it, they will simply return to their former state.
Since one who has entered the first *koṭī* (stage) has not yet reached the state of the final mind of the stage shared with bodhisattvas,

it is not the case that a bodhisattva who has heard and reflected upon the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is not practicing well. If it were said that failing to hear or understand this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* constitutes a lack of skillful practice,
then hearing, understanding, and reflecting upon the *Vimalakīrti*, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Laṅkāvatāra*, and the *Saṃdhinirmocana* would all likewise not be skillful practices.

Question: Regarding the passage in the sutra from "there being sentient beings" up to "attaining perfect enlightenment," what is its meaning? Answer: Seeing and hearing this sutra brings one close to the first stage of right awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Hearing it constitutes the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*); believing and understanding it constitutes the wisdom of reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*); and receiving and maintaining it constitutes the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*).
Now, concerning this section, there have been three general divisions above; however, in the middle division alone, there is only the mention of "explaining" and so forth.
In both the preceding and following passages, there are mentions of "reciting" (*dhāraṇī*) and "copying"; are these all instances of the cultivation of wisdom (*bhāvanā-prajñā*)?
How could that which is received and maintained not be called the cultivation of wisdom? And how could copying be entirely devoid of wisdom?

In many previous texts, it is stated that the seventh stage is equal to the two vehicles regarding birth-and-death within the realm of segmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*). Why, then, in this context, is it said to be close to perfect enlightenment? Is this not a contradiction?

If one subdues the afflictions prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and attains perfect enlightenment immediately upon the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), then is the first stage "Joyful" (*pramuditā*) or is it "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-jñāna*)?

In the *Avataṃsaka*, it is said that one already attains the Dharma-body at the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*); why, then, is it stated here that one only approaches perfect enlightenment upon entering the stages?
Question: In the *Sūtra*, it says, "O Bhaiṣajyarāja, for example, when one knows that water must be near," what does this mean? Answer: The *Śāstra* states: This is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature;
because it brings about the realization of Bodhi, it refers to the principle-nature (*li-xing*) expounded by the teaching, which is the Bodhi of the First Ground that must be sought and pursued.
Guangping said: Originally, the metaphor refers to the Buddha’s True Dharma, which covers the four modes of birth and, amidst the myriad phenomena, transcends all paths.
Difficult to ascend is the high plateau; taking the external teachings as the plain, within that plain there is a high plateau.
Taking wondrous wisdom as the precursor and the three karmas as the instruments, one discriminates, investigates, and seeks Bodhi.

Because the former teachings of the Two Vehicles lacked the mark of Great Enlightenment, they are called "water far away. For those who apply effort without ceasing, the two benefits [of self and others] do not stop.
The teaching of Prajñā-emptiness is like moist soil because it possesses the potential for Bodhi; therefore, hearing this sutra is like knowing that water must be near.

This reveals that the teachings of the Two Vehicles are considered distant, while the Mahāyāna teachings are considered near; the teaching of emptiness is considered remote, while the Middle Teaching is considered intimate.
Now I ask: is the True Dharma the plain land, and are the external teachings the level valley? Since there is a plain land within a level valley, it should be so.

If non-Buddhists and those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) previously sought the Dharma for Bodhi by means of wisdom’s discernment at some location, prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where else could that "previous time" have been indicated?

If those of the Two Vehicles already possessed the two benefits (svārtha and parārtha), why would they need to further turn their minds toward seeking the Great Vehicle? Since their [former] minds were already dead in the past, where could they possibly give [the gift of the Dharma]?

If merit is not yet perfected, what is the difference between emptiness within the *prajñā* and that of the Lesser Vehicle? Why is there no "emptiness within emptiness" in the *prajñā*, and toward what does the teaching further point?
If the present teaching were this [ultimate] emptiness, one should perceive water directly; why then do you merely speak of "intimacy"?
Since the *prajñā* itself possesses moisture and the potential for *bodhi*, how does it concern the Two Vehicles? Furthermore, as for what you call "potential," is it already [actualized]?

If those who have not yet resolved their minds [to attain enlightenment] do so [by means of this teaching], and for those who have already resolved their minds, why would they need the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?

Question: From the passage "For what reason? (*tat kasya hetoḥ*) until "it is for the sake of revealing and showing" (*saṃdarśayituṃ vyākaraṇāya ca*), what is the meaning? Answer: The Dharma of Great Bodhi possesses causes and fruits;

it has both proximate direct causes and remote indirect causes. These include the teachings (*śāsana*), principles (*yukti*), practices (*caryā*), fruits (*phala*), as well as wisdom (*jñāna*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and nature (*svabhāva*).

The five kinds of wisdom all belong to this sūtra; because they are attained through this sūtra and are subsumed within it, the "opening of the gate of expedient means" subsumes the distant and peripheral teachings on the doctrine, principle, practice, and fruit of the two vehicles (dvayayāna) taught in the past.

The "revealing of the true aspect" subsumes the proximate and direct teachings on the doctrine, principle, practice, and fruit of the one vehicle (ekayāna) taught in the present, encompassing them all completely. Thus, [the five wisdoms] are all subsumed within this sūtra.

Question: One should open the door before revealing the truth; if it is opened and then shown, that which was distant becomes near and that which was indirect becomes direct. In this sutra, which passage opens [the door] first without yet showing [the truth], and in which scriptural passage is it finally shown? If you point to the "Expedient Means" chapter, where the Buddhas of the three periods speak of the three carts, the single cart, the illusory city, and the precious destination, as being the opening: [Response: That is not so. In that chapter, the Buddha merely reveals the ultimate fruit of the Great Vehicle for those who have already entered the path of the Bodhisattva. It does not reveal the ultimate fruit for those who have not yet entered the path of the Bodhisattva. Therefore, that is not the opening of the door. Furthermore, in that chapter, the Buddha does not yet reveal the ultimate fruit for those who have already entered the path of the Śrāvaka. Consequently, that too is not the opening of the door. Moreover, in that chapter, the Buddha does not yet reveal the ultimate fruit for those who have already entered the path of the Pratyekabuddha. Consequently, that too is not the opening of the door. Furthermore, in that chapter, the Buddha does not yet reveal the ultimate fruit for those who have already entered the path of the Mahāyāna. Consequently, that too is not the opening of the door. Moreover, in that chapter, the Buddha does not yet reveal the ultimate fruit for those who have already entered the path of the Three Vehicles. Consequently, that too is not the opening of the door. Furthermore, in that chapter, the Buddha does not yet reveal the ultimate fruit for those who have already entered the path of the Two Vehicles. Consequently, that too is not the opening of the door. Moreover, in that chapter, the Buddha does not yet reveal the ultimate fruit for those who have already entered the path of the One Vehicle. Consequently, that too is not the opening of the door. Furthermore, in that chapter, the Buddha does not yet reveal the ultimate fruit for those who have already entered the path of the Four Vehicles. Consequently, that too is not the opening of the door. Moreover, in that chapter, the Buddha does not yet reveal the ultimate fruit for those who have already entered the path of the Five Vehicles. Consequently, that too is not the opening of the door. Furthermore, in that chapter, the Buddha does not yet reveal the ultimate fruit for those who have already entered the path of the Six Vehicles. Consequently, that too is not the opening of the door. Moreover, in that chapter, the Buddha does not yet reveal the ultimate fruit for those who have already entered the path of the Seven Vehicles. Consequently, that too is not the opening of the door. Furthermore, in that chapter, the Buddha does not yet reveal the ultimate fruit for those who have already entered the path of the Eight Vehicles. Consequently, that too is not the opening of the door. Moreover, in that chapter, the Buddha does not yet reveal the ultimate fruit for those who have already entered the path of the Nine Vehicles. Consequently, that too is not the opening of the door. Furthermore, in that chapter, the Buddha does not yet reveal the ultimate fruit for those who have already entered the path of the Ten Vehicles. Consequently, that too is not the opening of the door. Moreover, in that chapter, the Buddha does not yet reveal the ultimate fruit for those who have already entered the path of the Eleven Vehicles. Consequently, that too is not the opening of the door. Furthermore, in that chapter, the Buddha does not yet reveal the ultimate fruit for those who have already entered the path of the Twelve Vehicles. Consequently, that too is not the opening of the door. Moreover, in that chapter, the Buddha does not yet reveal the ultimate fruit for those who have already entered the path of the Thirteen Vehicles. Consequently, that too is not the opening of the door. Furthermore, in that chapter, the Buddha does not yet reveal the ultimate fruit for those who have already entered the path of the Fourteen Vehicles. Consequently, that too is not the opening of the door. This explains how the four dharmas of immeasurable meaning are distributed; herein it is said that these four dharmas are complete. Question:
What is the meaning of the scripture’s statement that they are "profound, firm, and remote"? Answer: "Profound" means subtle and difficult to fathom;

"firm" means indestructible, for they are realized through sublime wisdom by cultivating causes over great eons, and since no one other than a Buddha can achieve them, there is no one who can [destroy them]. No one.
Since he has been able to reach the ultimate limit of reality, he now manifests as a Bodhisattva and thus reveals this teaching.
As for the previous question—why was it said that he only transforms those who have regressed from the Mahāyāna and turned their minds [toward the Hīnayāna]?

If he were only transforming those of the Hīnayāna, why would the *Upāya-paṛivarta* state, "He only transforms all Bodhisattvas"? Because he is transforming Bodhisattvas, he does not transform only those Śrāvakas who have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna].
Therefore, we know that [those who hold such views] see but a single path; for if only a Buddha could reach the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi), they would have no share in it.

Thus, we know that this sutra is spoken by the Buddha for the sake of the Buddhas alone—what concern does it have with the lower stages? Why is it that the primary teaching is intended solely for those of the Two Vehicles, and to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision?
Question: What is the meaning of "entering the Tathāgata’s chamber" up to "sitting upon the seat of the emptiness of phenomena"?

Answer: It is the instruction on the ritual procedures as stated in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*: "When a person who preaches the Dharma occupies the lion throne, there are four dharmas they must observe:
first, they should first pay respectful homage to the assembly; second, if there are women in the assembly, they should contemplate their impurity; third, [their] deportment..."
In the rites, there are the characteristics of a great man: his countenance is harmonious and joyful; he does not delight in the scriptures of non-Buddhists; his mind is free from fear;

and fourth, when faced with malicious words or difficult challenges, he practices patience. Furthermore, there are four other dharmas: first, not disparaging oneself; second, not disparaging the listener;
third, not disparaging that which is taught; and fourth, not seeking profit or sustenance. Now, I say that these matters are most excellent indeed.

Furthermore, what is cited here is not appropriate for this sutra; this sutra—characterized by the robe of tranquil patience, the chamber of great compassion, and the seat of the dharma-emptiness—cites [passages from] two and four [other texts], yet none of them explain the sutra.
(From the "Chapter on Seeing the Jeweled Stupa")
Question: What is the meaning of the initial arrival? Answer: As the treatise states, "The three equalities eliminate the three defiled forms of pride.

Regarding the three defiled forms of pride: first, believing that the various vehicles are different; second, believing that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are different; and third, believing that one's own body and another's body are different.
Regarding the three equalities: first is the equality of the vehicle, as previously explained. Now, since it says "as previously stated," this refers to—

The preceding chapter was not solely for the sake of the Dharma Master; if [the notion that] various vehicles have already been refuted, how could medicinal herbs be established with further distinctions?
Next, in order to eliminate the belief that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are different, it is said that the Tathāgata manifests the Jewel Stūpa even after his parinirvāṇa.
Third, in order to refute the distinction between this body and that body, it is shown that the Buddha Prabhūtaratna encompasses all Buddhas.
The *Śarīra-śāstra* states: "Briefly stated, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna manifests a single dharma-body that encompasses all Buddha-bodies;

because this body is equal, it is said that one body subsumes all bodies. Furthermore, the fact that two Buddhas sit together in the stupa reveals that there is no difference between the two bodies, for the emanated bodies of Śākyamuni and the assembled bodies are not distinct. Therefore, that Buddha’s body is precisely my own body."
Furthermore, among the ten unsurpassed manifestations discussed in the treatise, the fifth is the unsurpassed manifestation of the pure land.

It manifests the stupa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna rising up, the gathering of the emanated bodies of the Buddhas, and the Buddha emitting a single ray of light that reveals five hundred *koṭi-nayuta* lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to the east,
with lapis lazuli for their ground, each measuring four million *koṭis* on all eight sides.
Because the excellence of the Buddha-dharma is manifested through the purity of other lands, it is not limited to impure realms;
since even in pure Buddha-lands there is primordial purity, this chapter has come forth. Now, according to the commentary on the treatise, there is no dharma that is not understood.
Question: I have heard that there is an objection to this chapter which asks: "Why not base [the teaching] on a pure land when speaking for the sake of the two vehicles?

It is only after they have realized the Dharma that a pure land exists. Answer: This is because one wishes to show that the two vehicles are directed toward the Great Vehicle; thus, it is initially defiled and subsequently pure.
Now, if this were so, once the two vehicles had turned back [toward the Great Vehicle], they would never again regress, and their land should therefore be eternally pure.
Because it is not defiled, one knows that when the two vehicles receive their predictions, each receives a prediction for a pure land;

thus, one understands that the purity or impurity of the transformation lands is for the sake of sentient beings, rather than being a sign that must wait for such purity to be manifested. That they become temporarily pure and then return to impurity signifies the entry into reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
This is also seen within the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, where the Tathāgata presses the earth with his toe, causing it to become pure and then return to impurity, thereby providing further proof.
Because this is the first fruit [of the path], we know that the purity of the land in the present sutra represents the place where the emanated bodies sit to preach the Dharma;

it specifically represents the fact that those of the Two Vehicles, having already received their predictions, have entered the stage of non-arising patience (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and partially realized the Dharma-body, thereby entering the land of emptiness, which is why it is used as a representation.
This principle should be understood by analogy for all the lands seen through the emission of light within the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other texts, let alone the present case.

Furthermore, this manifestation of the stupa emerging as a proof of the power of the sutra has already caused those who are reached by it to enter the abode of quiescence; since they now abide in eternal tranquility, this serves as the demonstration, and no further explanation is required.
Question: For what reason does the Buddha manifest immeasurable bodies? Answer: The treatise states: "To manifest the various deeds performed for both [self and others]."
Because there is no distinction between them, and because that which is performed by the provisional at the beginning and the real at the end is identical;

it is now said that if, in the preceding introduction, what was seen through the light and Mañjuśrī’s citation of the ancient Buddhas’ responses already indicated that all [teachings] are provisional first and real later, then the present manifestation of the divided bodies is primarily for the purpose of opening the stupa—the stupa itself symbolizing only the realization of this revelation. If it were not opened, it would be in vain to speak thus.

What benefit is there in first employing provisional means and subsequently employing the ultimate reality for the purpose of opening up this profound intention? Therefore, one should know that what is expressed cannot be treated as mere uniformity.
Question: Someone asks, "For what reason did the stūpa leap up into the air without changing its earthly substance, and how did the emanated Buddhas assemble at the beginning?"

[Question: Is the land being transformed? [Answer: It is said that while Prabhūtaratna manifests the appearance of dwelling in an impure land to accord with the Two Vehicles, his division of the body (nirmāṇakāya) accords with the Bodhisattvas;
therefore, he first transforms the land into a pure land. Now, since it is said that Prabhūtaratna abides in the void, what need is there for a pure land?
His divided body is on the ground, so the land must be adorned. This adornment of the manifested site signifies that the abodes of all Buddhas are fundamentally pure lands.
The essence of the Dharma is manifested as empty space; since the assembly has newly realized this, they are all equal to that emptiness.

If one were to say that the presence of Prabhūtaratna indicates compliance with the two vehicles—thereby making the beginning impure and the end impure—or that his division of the body indicates compliance with the bodhisattvas—thereby making the beginning pure and the end pure—then when the land was pure, Prabhūtaratna was also in that pure land, and when the land was impure, the bodhisattvas were likewise in that same impurity and the same purity. Why is this so?
Furthermore, as for the distribution [of relics], the stūpa leapt into the air; it never resided in filth, so how could it reside in filth? This makes their objection equally difficult to sustain.
Moreover, they claim that the *Lotus Sūtra* is intended exclusively for those of the Two Vehicles, yet it causes all beings from beginning to end to dwell in impurity;

this contradicts the principle of initial defilement followed by subsequent purity. Furthermore, because Much Treasure (Prabhūtaratna) was present to hear the *Lotus Sūtra*, and since the sūtra universally benefits all, including bodhisattvas...

Regarding the term "śrāvaka," if one merely follows the śrāvakas while opposing the bodhisattvas, then because the purification of the land is not dedicated solely to the bodhisattvas, it is known that the meaning of "following" is not established.
Furthermore, it is said that because Prabhūtaratna occupies an impure land, he represents the initial stage of following the two vehicles;

whereas because his emanations occupy a pure land, they represent the subsequent stage of following the two vehicles. Now, I maintain that the meaning of the emanations following the subsequent stage has already been established.

As previously stated regarding the *Prabhūtaratna* [Sūtra], why would it accord with what precedes but not with what follows? Since it has already been explained that emptiness does not involve defilement, the purport of the two preceding and succeeding explanations is contradictory.
Furthermore, if the *Śrāvaka* and *Lotus Sūtra* were distinct in their sequence, at what stage would the Bodhisattvas originally have resided such that they are purified only later?
Moreover, since it is said that those from the seventh ground downward share in the "segmented" (*paricchinna*) existence, how could hearing this sūtra increase their merit?
If purity occurs only after the path has been established, it would be the same as that of the Two Vehicles; why then need it be explained separately?

Furthermore, if those of the Two Vehicles attained purity through hearing [the teaching], they should have already attained purity after the three weeks [of the Lotus Sūtra]; why then would it wait until this point for the gathering of the manifested bodies? Thus, one knows that [your position] is erroneous.
Question: Furthermore, some ask why the "host" transformations (*prabhu-vikāra*) are said to have three stages while the "guest" positions (*atithi-sthāna*) consist of only two.

Answer: This is to manifest that the number of divided bodies (*kāya-bheda*) is many; now we say this is not the answer. If the guests are many, what prevents there being three positions? Furthermore, it is said that this manifests the sequence reaching the third stage as the ultimate manifestation of this One Vehicle (*ekayāna*);
since the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*) reach their ultimate at the third stage, we now ask: if the pure [stage] reaches the third, does it signify the culmination of the three?
If this is so, should it not be that three are ultimate while one is not? Furthermore, it is said that the expedient means correspond to medicinal herbs:

the three, the one, and the two are all ultimate, yet they mutually negate one another before and after; thus, the three and the one are all non-ultimate. Therefore, we know that what is manifested by purity has no bearing on what is heard.

Moreover, it is said: "The original defilement manifests the stage of ordinary beings; the first transformation manifests the Śrāvaka; the second transformation manifests the Pratyekabuddha; and the third transformation [manifests the Buddha]."

The table [of categories] for the Bodhisattva extends from the second stage (*dvitīya-bhūmi*) to the fulfillment of the first stage (*ekāika-sthāna-paripūri*); thus, it is not numerous. Now, one asks:

why does the preceding corruption belong to the Śrāvaka, while this corruption belongs to the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)? Since there is no fixed standard for what is expressed, it is precisely because the interpretation is not [correct].

Even if one speaks of guest and host, or of the guest being numerous, this still does not constitute a correct answer. Therefore, whether the answer is "many" or "few," it is not an answer to the question of "two" or "three. Thus, it is not an answer.
Knowing that the three seats do not hinder multiplicity, and furthermore, if the three transformations were used to represent the three [vehicles], how could one person sit facing two or three?

Moreover, from the first transformation to the third, there is no difference in purity; yet since the meanings of what is severed by the three vehicles differ in depth and shallowness, it is known that the transformations cannot represent the three vehicles.
Furthermore, since this sutra already fundamentally unifies the three, why would it be necessary to use them again?

Third, this is separately presented as a formal exposition. Question: Furthermore, there is a question asking why the Guest Buddha sat down twice. Answer: It was because he wished to cause the three transformations to reach the Way.

Now, it is said that this too does not answer the question; because it does not answer, the question is posed again: "Why did he not sit down three times? Answer: [The reason is as follows:]... (text continues).

[The opponent] again claims that because the text and meaning of the *Lotus Sūtra* are profound, they must now be called "the third" [in the sequence], and thus the text and meaning should be shallow;
this is offered as an answer to the objection regarding incomprehensibility. Furthermore, [the opponent] states of their own accord that the seat of Prabhūtaratna is also the "third. I say:

When the original question concerned the three transformations of the seat, why bring up the transformation prior to the answer? If one relies on the wording of this question, there was originally no need to ask it; why then labor so hard to establish it?
The established response is likewise not clear. Now, I say that the guest Buddha sitting again symbolizes the correspondence between superiority and inferiority;

the three purities are no different from the symbols of the three perfect wisdoms. The three delusions are completely shattered, and all Buddhas upon whom one relies do so by means of the three truths.

The three wisdoms of the Buddhas who can sit are without deficiency. Since Much Treasure (Prabhūtaratna) was already situated within true emptiness previously, to wish to see Much Treasure, one must realize the three purities.
Therefore, we know that without possessing the three types of wisdom, one cannot perceive [the truth], and without destroying the three delusions, one cannot open [to it].

Question: Regarding the passage in the sutra from "only leaving this assembly" to "other lands," how is this to be understood? Answer: Those who are capable of hearing [the teaching] and possess the karmic affinity remain;
those who are incapable of hearing and lack the affinity depart. Now, it is said that beyond the three thousandfold world-system, four hundred worlds are shifted in each of the eight directions.
Regarding these ten trillion beings, they are currently outside the transformation-realm of Śākyamuni; fundamentally, it has not been discussed whether they possess the karmic affinity or not.
Why, then, are they brought forward to discuss their suitability? Furthermore, why are the eight classes of supernatural beings present in the assembly while the humans and devas are moved elsewhere?
There must be a reason for this, yet no judgment has been made upon it.
Question: Furthermore, someone asks why each of the Buddhas has only one attendant. Answer: It is simply because when opening the stūpa, there is no need for attendants to transmit messages;

the ritual procedure is sufficiently managed by a single person. Now, while it is indeed true that a single person is sufficient for transmitting the ritual procedure, this is not a stable or convenient principle when facing the task of opening the stūpa.
According to the principle of opening the stūpa, it is necessary to assemble the emanated bodies (nirmāṇakāya).

In principle, the emanated bodies (nirmāṇakāya) should have attendants; while there may appear to be distinctions between those who are close and those who are distant, it is not the case that they do not rely on one another at all.

Thus, a single attendant represents a retinue free from confusion, and both master and attendant together serve as the conditions for opening the stupa. Furthermore, when asked, "Where does the attendant sit?

the answer was, "Why must he sit? Now, I say that because the śrāvakas of the Shared Teaching (sādhāraṇa-yāna) are proximate to the Buddha in their traces, they are therefore made to sit, whereas the Bodhisattvas...
Because the physical forms and rituals [of the two vehicles] are distant from one another, it is established that while Bodhisattvas of the Mahāyāna sit [within the stupa], Śrāvakas stand [outside].

It is logically consistent for an attendant here to transmit a message or express consent (*chanda*). Since there is no textual passage concerning the "returning after not having turned back," the matter of opening the stupa is collectively accomplished.

Thus, they sit together upon the same empty seat, equally manifesting the *sambhogakāya* light; since the place where they sit is so lofty and profound, how can it be said that [the Śrāvakas] do not [participate]?
[Mañjuśrī] sat down. Again it is said: "Vimalakīrti awaited the guest; Kṣemadatta [borrowed] from King Dīpaṃkara, and Śākyamuni extended hospitality to his attendants.

Because there were no seats, he answered that while those are for the laity, these are for the Buddha, and thus they are not the same. Now I say: Vimalakīrti made the Lesser Vehicle feel inferior by means of the empty room;

now, to manifest his own emptiness and quiescence, he borrowed seats from King Dīpaṃkara. This was to humble the ignorant of the Lesser Vehicle, and having refuted them, he restored [the seats] to them. If one says...

According to worldly custom, one should prepare seats to attend to guests. How do we know that the guest was expected to arrive? The date and time were approaching, yet the midday meal was suddenly unprepared;

instead of providing what was required, one blames the guest for the lack of beds and seats, shifting the fault onto another. Therefore, we know that such worldly sentiments should not be applied here.

Furthermore, it is said that there are five ways in which the earth may be transformed. One: * *The original text fragment provided ends with "一" (one), indicating the first item of a list regarding the transformation of the earth.*
1. Transforming the dimensions of the land; 2. Transforming the arising of evil; 3. Transforming the pure characteristics; 4. Transforming the evil land; 5. Transforming the adornment of the land.

Now, regarding these, it may be acceptable that the dimensions and characteristics are as described in the sutra; however, the "arising" involves shifting rather than transformation, and the "adornment" refers to something newly arriving. Furthermore, the subsequent passage states:
"Causing all bodhisattvas to scatter flowers upon Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa," which implies that the assembly site itself is not transformed. This refers to the preceding section.
To claim that only this assembly was left behind is logically untenable. As the preceding text states, "only those who were capable of hearing the Dharma were left";

how could it wait for the transformation of the impure realm before leaving the defiled one to show it to visitors? Furthermore, to say this is also incorrect; speaking according to reality, the mountain itself was transformed, and the scattering of flowers was merely a way of retaining the old name.
Now, I consider this interpretation to be excellent, though it still carries a trace of worldly sentiment; yet, even if the numinous presence were to remain...
The mountains have few impurities to represent the realm of ancient transformation; how could they feel the shame of a guest when facing the various Buddhas of the manifested body?
There is no loss in remaining as it was, for the mountains have not yet been moved. Furthermore, it is said: covering the impure with the pure is called "moving";
seeing impurity before generating the aspiration [for enlightenment] and seeing purity after generating that aspiration is called "moving. This is the movement of appearances.

Because it concerns the mind, one speaks only of "shifting the devas and humans" and not of "shifting the locations. Now, since the location fundamentally does not shift, why must you raise this objection?

Furthermore, if it is not called "transformation," what need is there for such circuitous refutation? Generally speaking, that which is called "concealment" (āvṛti) is when the impurity remains below while, later on, a new pure *karma* arrives;
because there is both a departure and an arrival, it is termed "concealment. Moreover, as for what is called "concealment," purity follows from...
Because he obtains defilement again and departs with it, it is called "concealment" (*āvṛti*); were it not so, its establishment would be merely laborious and empty.

Furthermore, as for the mind and its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), one may only speak of their "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) and should not speak of their "transfer. Moreover, if gods and humans merely transferred their mental characteristics, this would also contradict the sūtras;

for the sūtras explicitly state that "transfer" refers to the transfer of the body—how then could it be called a transfer of characteristics? Therefore, one should simply follow the scriptural teachings and principles.
The two phenomena—the mountain remaining as it was and the multitude having moved—are starkly evident; how could they be unrelated to the discernment of the mind?
To say that the purity is revealed through the manifestation of the hidden is to say that when Mañjuśrī wished to go to Mount Hua, where was the mountain?

Once the mountain had already been moved, if one were to claim it did not move, it would still be there just as before. Now, since you have already used the phrase "as if," is this not a failure to reach a definitive conclusion from the outset?
One should know that this was originally a matter of hesitation; why must one insist on resolving it? Regarding the term "yào" (key): the *Yùpiān* states it refers to a door bolt.
In the region east of the Pass, it is called a "jiàn" (bolt), while in the region west of the Pass, it is called a "yào" (key). These are merely archaic characters.
Question: Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "Śākyamuni" up to "sitting in the full lotus posture," what is its meaning? Answer:

The Treatise states that it is to manifest transformation-buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*), non-transformation-dharma-buddhas, reward-buddhas (*saṃbhoga-buddha*), and so forth, all for the sake of accomplishing the Great Matter; this is precisely the "one great causal condition" (*ekamahā-kāraṇa*).
It further states that it signifies the three vehicles (*triyāna*) together sitting upon the seat of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Now, I say that the person is the one who relies upon the seat.

Regarding this basis, if one examines it from the perspective of the factual (vastu), what is so strange about a person of the Two Vehicles who has left the household life sitting on the same couch as a Bodhisattva?

However, if one examines it from the perspective of principle, is liberation attained through the objective (ālambana) or the subjective (ālambaka)? Since the objects of liberation—the afflictions (*kleśa*)—and the attainment of emptiness are distinct, how could those being liberated be the same?
If it is argued that prior to the seventh stage, they are equal to the Two Vehicles and thus their names are the same; [this is not so].
As for those who sit, this refers to the common stage of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, which is insufficient to explain the ritual of sitting together;
were it the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where even the designation of "three vehicles" no longer exists, one likewise could not establish the statement that they sit together.

Question: Regarding the sutra’s statement that "exquisite fragrance issues from the body, causing the Dharma to abide for a long time," what does this mean? Answer: It reveals that the body emits fragrance to benefit sentient beings through the preaching of the Dharma;

this may be the fragrance emitted by Śākyamuni himself, or it may be emitted by the emanation-buddhas (*nirmāṇakāya*). At first glance, reading the text, it appears to be the emanation-buddhas who emit it.
In the prose section, there is only mention of Śākyamuni burning incense to await guests; it is not the guests who emit fragrance to await him.
The Master now says that the common sentiments of recent times are like those of worldly people setting out food for guests; what further fault could there be?
Therefore, the common sentiments of recent times do not accord with the sacred principles of the Śākya Sage.
Question: From the passage in the Sūtra beginning with "from other various sūtras" up to "this constitutes a difficulty," what is the meaning? Answer: In total, there are six [points].

Regarding the refutations, they all have counterparts: the first five lines explain the difficulty of preaching; the next two lines record the difficulty of writing; the next two lines concern the difficulty of reading;
the next two lines concern the difficulty of preaching; the next three lines concern the difficulty of listening; and the final five lines concern the difficulty of upholding.

Now, while it is excellent that the text is thus divided, why is the reason for these refutations not described? Is this the case for all sutras, or is it unique to this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*? If [it is unique],...
If other sutras are likewise so, why is it that this one alone possesses such a quality and does not say the same?
Question: The sutra states, "If there is anyone who can uphold this, they uphold the body of the Buddha. Why is this so? Answer: This concludes the excellence of upholding [this specific sutra].
Now, why is it not explained what the reason is for upholding it being called "upholding the body of the Buddha"? If one upholds other sutras, they uphold the Buddha... [text ends]

[The interlocutor asks: "Is it not so? [The questioner asks: "In the sutra, from the time after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa until the point where it says 'one should make offerings,' what does this mean? [The respondent] answers:
"As a verse in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: 'If one were to carry the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world upon one's head for an entire kalpa without moving, the merit of that person...'"
To perform such deeds is not difficult; rather, it is for one who believes in this Dharma that this is difficult.

Even if all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm were to provide every kind of offering and pleasure, their merit would not be difficult to attain; it is for one who believes in this Dharma that it is truly supreme.
If one were to hold the lands of the ten directions in the palm of one's hand and remain suspended in mid-air for an eon, what they have accomplished would still not be difficult.

For those who believe in this Dharma, it is exceedingly difficult. Even if one were to provide all the various articles of pleasure as offerings to beings as numerous as the atoms within ten Buddha-fields, that merit would not be considered difficult; rather, believing in this Dharma is truly supreme.
Now, this "supremacy" is used to praise that sutra—is that sutra this very sutra, or is it not? If it is different, why is it cited here?

If this refers to the present sutra, how can one distinguish its differences? Moreover, while the *Avataṃsaka* merely compares [other teachings] in terms of merit, this sutra compares them in terms of the Dharma;
therefore it says, "even if one does not accept a single verse of another sutra. What benefit is there for those who do not reflect on this to cite such examples?

Question: What is the meaning of the "Devadatta Chapter" and the "Chapter on Questions"? Answer: The *Śāstra* states that among the six types of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), this is the "prediction of no enmity.

Now, I say that "no enmity" clarifies that enmity is fundamentally non-existent; it is not the case that one first establishes a state of being without enmity and only then provides the prediction. Furthermore, it is said to manifest the upholder [of the Dharma].
Because she is worthy of respect; furthermore, it is to manifest that this sūtra brings swift attainment of the Way.

That is, this very dragon girl is [the one spoken of] now—why then do you not say it is to manifest the lineage of teachers, to manifest the cause for the wondrous fruit, to manifest the great benefit gained from hearing this chapter, or to reveal that Devadatta was not fixed in evil?
It is to manifest that the lineages inherited by the Buddha’s disciples differ.
Question: What is the meaning of the name of this chapter? Answer: He was the son of Ghaṭīkāra, the younger brother of the Buddha’s maternal uncle.
Because he obtained [the name] from heaven, he is called Devadatta. Now, if one were to provide a direct explanation in this way, it would contradict the following text;
for if he had obtained it from heaven in this world, he should not have become the teacher of Śākyamuni. Therefore, one must say that Devadatta was a manifestation who verified heaven.
However, since the principle ought to be that which bestows the source of all phenomena, one knows that this sutra cannot be explained away with superficial ease.
Question: Someone has asked why, when this chapter contains the account of the Dragon Girl attaining Buddhahood, it is specifically called the "Chapter on Devadatta."

The answer is: The excellent conditions that led to Devadatta were the causes for Śākyamuni’s teachers; although others may appear superior, they were not the Buddha’s past causes, and therefore they are not titled as chapters.
Now, it is said that the titles of sutras and the names of chapters vary according to the circumstances—sometimes separate, sometimes combined—and both are acceptable in practice.
Furthermore, when the remaining text is extensive, it may also be designated with a distinct title.
Question: Someone asks why this chapter is not titled separately as "The Dragon Girl. Answer: Mañjuśrī is a virtuous friend who accords with conditions;
in various sūtras, he is sometimes identified as Devadatta. This is not the case here, however, because it is intended to manifest the gravity of the sūtra.

Thus, while the title of the chapter is established through an adverse condition (*viloma-pratyaya*), it is not established through a favorable condition (*anuloma-pratyaya*). Now, I say that this is not entirely so, for the meaning of this chapter is as follows:
To manifest the honored Dharma of Śākyamuni, the Teacher of Śākya, he cites the past events concerning Devadatta; to show that he would return, he leaves Jñānakuṭa behind;

to manifest that Mañjuśrī was due to arrive, he displays the excellence of the Dharma he holds; to verify that even one who has long been a beast can still attain Buddhahood in a mere moment, he uses the early realization as a proof;
and to distinguish the merit of his teaching, he employs the two conditions of compliance and opposition to contrast the titles of the chapters.
If even those who follow favorable conditions are not accorded the title of "Wondrous Sound" or "Avalokiteśvara Dharma Master," how much less so those who commit the five heinous crimes?

Furthermore, the conditions for committing such heinous acts in various teachings do not pertain to the original time of propagating the sutra; they are manifested within the provisional traces (*jise*) and are therefore distinct.
Thus, we know that the day one receives the sutra is still a time of favorable conditions, and it is not said to be a time of committing the heinous crimes.

The traces of Kōbō Daishi’s [Kūkai] actions—whether contrary or compliant—are diverse, yet his fundamental essence is not different because the conditions [of his teaching] are not different; therefore, his exhortation to uphold the sutras is not restricted solely to compliance or contrariety.

Why then would one discuss the fundamental based on the derivative? *Asura* (阿私) is translated here as "Incomparable" (*mubī*). Regarding the character *ruò* (蓏), its phonetic value is *guǒ* (菓), though it is sometimes read with the sound *gū* (苽).

Now, it is said that local dialects may render this vulgar; thus, the language of the sutras cannot be arbitrarily altered according to the criticisms of various lands, but must be adapted as appropriate.
Furthermore, the *Shanyupian* states: "Guo" refers to the category of peaches, plums, and the like; "luo" refers to the category of melons and gourds.
It further says that those with seeds are called "guo," while those without seeds are called "luo. Again, it says that the fruit of trees is called "guo," while the fruit of plants is called "luo.
It also says that what grows upon trees is "guo," while what grows upon the ground is "luo."

Question: Someone asks why Zhijī (Jñānaskandha) addressed the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, yet Śākyamuni remained behind. Answer: He addressed Prabhūtaratna because he was waiting for [the latter] to invite him back;
this follows the etiquette between host and guest. As for Śākyamuni remaining behind, although this accords with worldly custom, it is not without principle.
He wished to return and therefore addressed his original Buddha; logically, this is appropriate. His staying behind belongs to the category of benefiting others.
The condition was not simply that the guest and host, the attendant and disciple, must exist for one to follow the teacher and deeply master external decorum;

rather, it was established so that one might know how to realize the truth through application to things. Since the prior announcement had already been made and the departure was understood, the subsequent announcement was made upon returning. Therefore, the Buddha retained him to wait for Miaode.
Furthermore, someone asked about the beginning and end of the sutra. The answer is that [the Buddha] was present throughout the assembly; why, then, did it only now emerge from the Dragon Palace?

The answer is that the benefits for sentient beings are manifold, and whether he departs or remains, all are benefited. When the Buddha first preached the One Vehicle, he immediately concealed it and did not let it appear.

Now, as a verification of this, it has emerged from the Dragon Palace. It is said that while there is a slight discrepancy here compared to ancient traditions, this is due to the specific conditions of the current occasion.
The sutra contains no words of departure; therefore, the assembly collectively harbors doubt, wondering only why it was first preached and then concealed—how could this resolve their doubts?
It is merely that the deeds of the Dharma King are difficult to fathom. Thus, how could the essence of the oceanic assembly wait for this return?

Since two bodies cannot be established simultaneously, he remains hidden here while manifesting there; it is not a case of hiding what is already hidden. This requires being formless, coming without coming.

Regarding the statement that [the Buddhas] emerge from the ocean, it would be appropriate for them to appear together; however, if they were suddenly to manifest as emanations all at once, it would be inappropriate.
This is as the Buddha taught regarding their cessation. Furthermore, someone asked: "Since the emanated bodies (nirmāṇakāya) already exist, why do only two Honored Ones appear?

Why does Mañjuśrī alone pay homage to these two sages? The answer is: one returns specifically to those who are nearby; it is not necessarily required to pay homage universally. Thus, we know that the sages of the East specifically pay homage to these two.
Venerable One, as for the Bodhisattva Ratnaśrī of the Western Quarter, although his divided body remains, what fault could there be in this?
Now, if one were to say that since the divided body is present, the principle is not at fault, yet because he has already departed, the dialogue cannot be established;

therefore, it is not appropriate to use the gift of jewels as an analogy. If one were to use the gift of jewels as an analogy, taking the later to exemplify the former is truly unreasonable when examined.
The distribution of the precious jewels was divided into two parts; one part had already been distributed among the emanations, while the other part had not yet been returned to them.
This is why Mañjuśrī was not like that: when Mañjuśrī arrived, the stūpa had not yet been closed. Thus it is said: "I pay homage at the feet of the Two World-Honored Ones.

The two meanings of "coming from the East" and "sage of the West" are eternally distinct. When Gadgadasvara arrived, he requested Śākyamuni to manifest Avalokiteśvara’s distribution of the precious jewels and the [distribution of] the stūpa.
Since they are not non-human beings, they still abide within the two conditions [or gates]; the various Buddhas who manifest divided bodies return by means of this.
To cite them as a parallel would be an extreme error.
Question: From the passage concerning the Bodhisattva Zhiji (Jñānākūṭa) onwards, how many sections are there, and what is their textual content?

Answer: There are two benefits: first, the rapid attainment of the Way; second, the transformation of evil bodies—namely, the shedding of animal forms and the transformation of female natures—all of which are brought about by this sūtra.
Now, if Śāriputra has received his prediction [of future Buddhahood], why is it that the eight classes of beings have not yet done so? Why is this?
If a woman alone can attain perfect enlightenment, how much more so should it be for the fourfold assembly of human beings, none of whom lack the capacity?

Furthermore, when humans and animals are compared, what is the reason for this disparity? Moreover, since this dragon girl had previously obtained the power of the sutra, she should have already attained realization;

why then did she wait until the assembly to offer a pearl as a token of her swift attainment? What connection does the offering of the pearl have with the power of the sutra to bring about such realization? Such points are rarely heard.

Regarding the decision that other sutras are also like this—not only the Lotus Sutra—if it were only the Lotus Sutra [to be so], then since Śākyamuni was formerly a prince and had not yet declared his attainment of Buddhahood, he would still have been concealing his preaching of the sutra when he first began teaching it in the eight directions;
if other sutras were also like this, what would there be to marvel at? This is because of the passage where Zhijixian asks for a separate method to quickly attain [the goal].

This distinction is cited as evidence that [the Bodhisattva] attained the vision of the Buddha swiftly; yet when he offered the pearl, the five obstacles and his doubts were exhausted, and he suddenly transformed to travel directly to the south.
Why was Śākyamuni so slow? He passed through kalpas of dust and sand—could it be that the Prince’s propagation of the Dharma was inferior to that of the female animal?
Please provide an answer.
Question: The Sūtra says, "The benevolent go; what is meant by 'the benevolent'? Answer: The *Zhou Li* states that the benevolent possess six virtues.

The first is benevolence (*ren*). Zheng Xuan explains: "Loving people and all things is called benevolence. "Superiors and subordinates being affectionate toward one another is called benevolence. "Valuing the worthy and showing kinship to one's own kin is called benevolence.

"Sacrificing one's life to complete another person is called benevolence. As for the benevolent, they are patient (*ren*); they cherish life and loathe killing, embracing both good and evil within themselves.
Ren said, "This is the benevolence of an ordinary person, not the virtue of Mañjuśrī. What is there that would be improper about combining it with Mañjuśrī’s supreme virtues?
He asked, "What can one attain by reaching Mañjuśrī? He replied, "In Mañjuśrī’s answer, there are sixteen virtues."
1. A dragon; 2. Two daughters; 3. Small; 4. Wisdom and sharpness; 5. Knowledge of the faculties (*indriya*); 6. Attainment of *dhāraṇī*, which is the ability to hear and retain;
7. Attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); 8. Comprehension of the Dharma; 9. Non-retrogression; 10. Eloquence (*pratibhāna*); 11.
Compassionate mindfulness; 12. Endowment with virtue; 13. Swift eloquence; 14. Profundity and distance of what is taught; 15. Benevolence, kindness, and humility; 16. Harmony.
Master Ya now says that these sixteen virtues cannot manifest [the state of] swift attainment; yet since they are listed in the Sūtra, there must be a profound intention behind them.

With the exception of the first and second, the others require a distinction to be made: although the first two are excluded, one might ask why they are placed among the dragons (*nāgas*) when they still have a small remainder [of defilements], while the fourteen [remaining virtues] cause one to achieve swift accomplishment.
If it were solely on the basis of the Sūtra, who would not obtain the status of an Arhat and receive their prediction (*vyākaraṇa*)?
Question: Having made offerings to the Buddhas throughout kalpas, how can this female animal so quickly achieve success?

Please answer. Question: From Śāriputra’s inquiry until this point, for what reason is it said that this matter is difficult to believe? Answer: Śāriputra raised his doubts; as for the subsequent passage from "Why is this?
to "quickly attaining Buddhahood," the explanation is: one body is defiled and cannot [attain realization] at two different times.

One cannot avoid the three obstructions, nor can one be too heavy with them. Furthermore, as stated in the *Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Sun’s Transcendent Radiance*, the Bhikṣu Shangdu said to Hui-shi:
"A woman cannot attain Buddhahood because she is separated by three things and hindered by five things.
The three separations are: while at home one is dependent on one's parents; upon marriage, one is dependent on one's husband; and when the husband dies, one follows after his son."
This is also consistent with the secular texts' principle of "three obediences. Regarding the five matters, they are the same as today;

however, while those texts state that the Brahma King must possess pure conduct and the four immeasurables, the intent of the present text is as follows: because women desire what is weighty, Śakra must possess courage and vigor;
because women have many affectations, Māra must be fully endowed with the ten wholesome paths; and because women disparage the Three Jewels and their parents, teachers, and elders.
Because the teachings on pride [prohibit it], a Wheel-Turning King must cultivate the ten wholesome paths; because women lack pure conduct, they are currently questioned as follows:
since you have cited the scriptures at length to demonstrate that [women] cannot [attain Buddhahood], what causes and conditions allow a dragon girl to attain it?
If you point to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, what would her practice be like? Please answer.
Question: Why does the Sūtra state that the Dragon King’s daughter arrived here so swiftly? Answer: There are two aspects to the Dragon Girl’s attainment of Buddhahood:
first, the metaphor of offering the pearl; second, the demonstration of her actual attainment of Buddhahood. The first [aspect] is further divided into four parts:

(1) the offering of the pearl, (2) the counter-question, (3) the direct answer, and (4) the concluding metaphor. Now, regarding the offering of the pearl: how can it resolve the doubts of the two sages? If the two sages find this difficult...
If [the account] were correct, then the matter of the dragon girl would not be as it is; if the matter of the dragon girl were true, then the two sages would be difficult to refute.

If they were difficult to refute, then citing the sutra would lack a basis. When questioned about what was correct, the dragon girl remained silent and did not explain why she simply offered the pearl.
Please answer this.
Question: From the passage in the sutra concerning the assembly at that time up to the "Sublime Dharma" (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka), what is its meaning?

Answer: It is to manifest the attainment of enlightenment. Furthermore, there are two aspects: first, seeing the cause; second, seeing the fruit. Now, regarding the term "manifestation," it means that although [the Buddha] attained realization long ago, he manifests it as if for the first time now.

If it were only now that he had finally achieved it, how could there be cause and fruit? Thus, rather than resolving the doubts of Prajñākūṭa, [the text] simply states directly: ... [text continues] ... *Note: This excerpt appears to be a commentary on a section of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, specifically addressing the nature of the Buddha’s manifestation of his enlightenment.*
Regarding the request for an answer concerning cause and effect:
The question asks, "From the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* up to the *Sūtra of Bestowing Predictions*, what is [the purpose]? The answer is: It is simply so that both parties may benefit.
Now, if one asks which teaching, when heard, brings about the most rapid benefit—if one were to preach other teachings, how could they possibly lead to the causal practices of the *Lotus Sūtra*?
Those who have realized the practice of the Lotus Sutra and those who preach the Lotus Sutra swiftly—where do such benefactors of the masses come from?
Are they all those who have regressed from the Mahāyāna and turned their minds back [to it]? Please answer. ○ The Chapter on Encouraging the Preservation (Dhāraṇī-parivarta).

Question: What are the categories [of this chapter]? Answer: The Treatise states, "The power of upholding is threefold: namely, the Dharma-preacher, the Practice of Peaceful Living (Anrakugyō), and the Exhortation to Uphold.

The Commentary explains: "The 'Dharma-preacher' encompasses both the subject and the object; the 'Practice of Peaceful Living' refers only to that which is upheld; this present chapter refers only to the subject of upholding. Now, I say:

since the Treatise merely states that "the power of upholding is threefold," and the single character "upholding" (ji) applies to both subject and object, it is known that all three chapters [share this quality].

The "penetration" (*prativedha*) encompasses both the object and the subject. Since the Dharma Master is a teacher of persons, the "Dharma" is peace and bliss; this is the practice that relies upon the person who practices it.

The exhortation to uphold [the Dharma] clearly implies both the subject and the object. Because the Dharma Master does not possess a dharma that is not the Dharma, peace and bliss are the fruit, while the practice is the means by which one approaches it.
One must rely on a person to reach the fruit; the practice is the cause, and the exhortation to uphold is that which the person exhorts, which is the Dharma.

How is it that you judge them one-sidedly, each claiming to be either the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*)? Question: Since this is the case for both agent and object, please further explain their names. Answer:

Because they maintain and sustain [the teaching] so that it does not perish, everything from copying to practicing is called "maintaining" (*dhāraṇa*). Now, since you have asked about "copying" and so forth—given that copying and such are the objects—what do you mean by this?

Regarding the term "able" (*neng*), it may also be translated simply as "to uphold" (*chi*); the meaning is likewise so. If one were to apply both terms [“exhortation” and “upholding”] together, it would mean that what was previously the Buddha’s exhortation is now being upheld.
Alternatively, it might be said that this chapter is the Buddha looking back and exhorting the Bodhisattvas to uphold it. Although this reasoning is not erroneous, many sutras have single titles.
Now, if you wish to rely on the treatise (*śāstra*), why do you not follow the treatise? Furthermore, to say that many sutras have single titles is incorrect.
If one must choose between being alone and being in pairs, it is better to be alone.

Question: Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "in an evil age" to "far removed from liberation," what is its meaning? Answer: It clarifies that there are six kinds of evil: first, the land; second, birth;
third, the arising of faculties; fourth, abundant afflictions; fifth, craving for fame and profit; and sixth, the lack of desire for liberation.
Now, although these six evils are thus, it should be said that they arise from conditions and are directed toward those who are ready to be transformed.
Question: From the passage in the Sūtra beginning with "Furthermore" up to "unreal," what is the meaning? Answer: This land possesses eight evils: first, evil in location;
second, evil in people; third, evil in pride; fourth, evil in virtue; fifth, evil in anger; sixth, evil in turbidity; [seventh, evil in views]; and eighth, evil in proximity to non-Buddhists.

Seventh, because of the arising of flattery and evil through the practice of flattery; eighth, the untruthful. Now it is asked: since these are all within this same land, why are the first six [not included] while this is designated as the eighth?
[The *Anlehangpin* (Chapter on Peaceful Practices)]

Question: What is the meaning and principle of the subsequent sections of this chapter? Answer: Among the three types of circulation (*pravartana*), the preceding four chapters constitute the circulation through praise and veneration;

these following seven chapters constitute the circulation through learning and practice (*śikṣā-pratipatti*). Now, one asks: since learning and practice belong to the subject (*kartṛ*), how can they belong to the object (*karman*)?

Furthermore, it is said: although the scripture has already been praised and venerated previously, if the practice of learning and performing the propagation of the sutra is not explained, many in the final age [will fail].

If it is difficult for injuries and destruction to arise frequently and one cannot widely propagate [the teaching], judging by this interpretation, how could it be determined that [this passage] belongs to the "object"? Furthermore, it is said:

"Among the seven categories, the single category of 'peaceful bliss' (anurakṣaṇā) is the practice of learning the sūtra; the six [categories] such as 'reciting' and 'explaining' are the persons who can uphold the sūtra.
A person achieves virtue through the Dharma, while the Dharma relies on persons for its wide propagation. If there were no practice of what is to be learned..."
