By what means does that person establish virtue so as to find peace and joy in the practice they have studied?

If there were no one capable of practicing it, by what means could this Dharma be widely disseminated? Now, if it is claimed that this chapter constitutes the practice for propagating the sutra, that may well be so;
however, it is not as previously explained—that Śāriputra, Mañjuśrī, and Maitreya serve as the presiding petitioners in three locations. This is not the case.

What is meant by this? Generally speaking, all instances of "requesting" refer to requesting the primary [teaching]. Here, it is judged that this passage belongs to the section on dissemination (*pravartana*).
Mañjuśrī merely asks: "In the future evil age, how can bodhisattva-mahāsattvas preach this sutra? Thus, one knows that this cannot be considered the prologue (*nidāna*) of the sutra.
Since the prologue occurs at the beginning while the section on dissemination comes at the end, they are not comparable. Therefore...

Knowing that the "Practice of Peaceful Conduct" (*Anrakugyō*) is the beginning of the Trace Gate (*jikimon*), how can one explain the statement in the *Trace Sūtra* (*jikikyō*) that it is the practice of the "Emanated Bodhisattvas" (*yūshutsu bosatsu*)?
It is said that this causes them to long perfect their original ground (*honji*) by returning to study the initial practices within the Trace.

If they were truly studying the initial practices within the Trace, why would Maitreya not recognize even a single person and instead ask, "From whom did you receive and uphold this sūtra? and inquire about its compilation?

From what source do the Buddha-dharmas arise? From whom does the aspiration for enlightenment (bodhicitta) originate? The Tathāgata answers by explaining the parable of the physician, the father, and the sons—one young and one old—and how [the Buddha] dwells, enters, and emerges from hundreds of thousands of samādhis. How can it be said that the Buddha-dharmas were gathered here at Gayā?
It is only when one begins to depart from adverse conditions and ceases to speak of the likes, dislikes, merits, or faults of others that one will first dream of entering [the path].

Venerable ones, since the "Chapter on Lifespan" speaks only of the Tathāgata’s original ground—his long-term accomplishment and his ancient retinue—how could one instead study the initial practices of his traces?
It would be like teaching a great-grandson to read the *Classic of Filial Piety* by using an eighty-year-old man as the model;

how could one expect the grandson to instead read that very text himself? Furthermore, the "Chapter on Distinguishing Merits" discusses only the benefits gained from hearing of [the Buddha's] long life.

How could the sutra ever have intended for one to study these four kinds of practice? Even if the dust of the eight realms were present, this initial aspiration to enlightenment is still "hearing from afar";

it is not an aspiration to enlightenment born of hearing the *Anrakugyō* (Peaceful Practices). As for the merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*), that was a comparison made by the person in the fiftieth place to illustrate the profound through the shallow;
the shallow dharma serves as the basis for the "Dharma Master" chapter, while the "Never-Disparaging" [Bodhisattva] clarifies his own past conduct.

To claim that by propagating a single phrase one attains the purification of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) is not to say that one is exclusively practicing the four practices for peaceful dwelling (*catvāraḥ sukhavihārāḥ*).
If one speaks from a universal perspective, citing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as the source, then this may indeed be acceptable.

Furthermore, since the various chapters prior to those of the Learners (*śaikṣa*) and Non-learners (*aśaikṣa*) constitute the One Reality solely for the sake of the Śrāvakas, how could it be that the Bodhisattvas who have long practiced and emerged from the earth would instead learn from the Śrāvakas to enter the practice of reality? This must be investigated thoroughly.
In the end, it remains unknown what constitutes the practice to be learned in the six categories. Furthermore, it is said that the *Śāstra* states:

"Regarding the sixth among the seven types of arrogant persons—the person who accumulates merit—it refers to preaching the Mahāyāna Dharma to one who possesses merit, yet who grasps at non-Mahāyāna through overweening pride (*adhimāna*);
for such a person, one preaches the 'precious pearl from within the topknot'. The commentary explains: "Those who seek the fruits of the three vehicles are called 'those who accumulate [merit]'."
In the past, those of merit spoke generally of the Mahāyāna; their minds were not yet settled, so they regressed to take up the Two Vehicles.

Having taken what is not the Mahāyāna, they obtained only minor merit and were granted mere residual things. Now, it is said in the treatise that these are simply "not the Mahāyāna," without mentioning "small.
This phrase "not [the] Great" carries a meaning that encompasses both the "Small" and the "Gradual," and so forth; it also includes the attainment of peace and bliss.
The practice of propagating the sūtras is not the antidote for the Mahāyāna; one should adopt this practice, whereas to regress and adopt the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is not the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, while the treatise merely states that the Mahāyāna dharma is taught, because this dharma-gate is identical to the fulfillment of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), it is explained that the Buddhas and Tathāgatas secretly bestow predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) upon those of the two vehicles, thereby causing them to share in the practices of the ten stages.
The "secret prediction" mentioned here refers to the teaching that the four practices of peaceful dwelling for a beginner are identical to the fulfillment of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*);
this is the meaning of the statement that "the initial resolve and the ultimate goal are not two different things. This principle is like the parable of bestowing a jewel:

if even a single phrase from the initial resolve is worthy of a prediction, how much more so for one who propagates the sutra? Thus, the fact that those of the two vehicles receive a prediction through the manifest teaching of this sutra is [the case].
The "subtle and profound mystery" is not a matter of secrecy. Question:
Among the four types of peaceful bliss (*sukha*), how many practices (*caryā*) are there? Answer: All four practices contain two [aspects], though they are explained only within the first practice.
Furthermore, it is said that there are two practices: one is delusion and the other is truth; thus, there should be no [separate] practice.
Having abandoned all deluded thoughts, one now speaks of the initial practice of contemplating the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This true mark is neither empty nor existent, neither real nor false;
since these four modes are collectively termed "peaceful bliss" (*anābhirati*), peaceful bliss is the fruit of these four practices.
Within each individual practice, all four propositions are fully present, yet they do not constitute those four propositions, because the fruit of the true mark is not comprised of the four.
Question: Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "the bodhisattva" to "the play of transformations," what is its meaning? Answer: Within this there are three [conditions]:
first, conditions of harm; second, conditions of wrong views; and third, conditions of disruption.

Although the bodhisattva acts as a condition for universal transformation, those who are beginners in practice should exercise discernment. Now, since it is said here that these are "beginners in practice," why are they divided [into these categories]?
The *Pin* (Chapter) says: "One should practice by leaping forth," and it further states that there are ten kinds of faults for entering a royal palace according to the Vinaya.
Regarding the Lord of Wu sharing a carriage, his fame lasted for a generation; regarding the Prince of Qin yielding his wife, he suffered shame for a thousand years.

Now you say that the Lord of Wu’s shared carriage brings eternal glory, yet the Prince of Qin’s yielding of his wife remains unfathomable after a thousand years. Why do you not admonish yourself and refrain from such disparaging criticism?
Since the worthy Nirgrantha outsider has already stated that these are the practices of the latter six stages, why would the multitude leaping from the earth require this admonition?
As for the terms "wen" (literature) and "bi" (writing), "wen" refers to genres such as poetry and song, while "bi" refers to works such as inscriptions on steles and biographies.
Regarding the term *Lokāyata*, it is said that they first speak ill and then answer others; the correct term is *Loka-āyatika*.
Regarding the term *Lokāyatika-vāmamārga-pratilomayātika*: it refers to those who pose malicious interrogations. It is correctly called *Vāmamārgayātika*.

As for the statement that the *Lokāyatika-vāmamārga* holds views contrary to the former, this means they are called "Left-hand Lokāyatas" because their doctrines pervade both of the aforementioned positions.
*Nara* refers to one who paints upon the body; *vikriyā-darśaka* refers to one who performs illusory arts (*māyā-karma*).
The *Āgama* states: "The wise always harbor sorrow like a prisoner in a jail; the foolish always rejoice like the devas of Ābhāsvara.

Now, if this [text] does not permit contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), upon what treatise is it based? Regarding the phrase "using the fist as a blade" (*chārèn jiāfǎn*), it means striking another with one's fist.
The scriptural text says: "Do not associate with those who lack restraint," referring to the *caṇḍāla*, which is translated here as "killer"; they are those who lack ethical discipline (*asaṃvara*).
The correct term is *caṇḍāla*, which here means "one who adorns themselves with evil deeds.
They take these as their insignia, shaking bells and carrying bamboo poles as their own marks. Among these, the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma* (Six-Footed Abhidharma) lists twelve types:
sheep-slaughterers, poultry-keepers, pig-keepers, fishers, bird-catchers, hunters, thieves, executioners, jailers, dragon-charmers, ox-slaughterers, dog-slaughterers, and spies.
16. Those who hunt for *nirvāṇa* (the following sixteen types): 1. One who buys fat cattle, sheep, pigs, or chickens for profit; 2. One who resells them for profit; 3.
One who slaughters them after buying them; 4. A fisherman; 5. A hunter; 6. A robber; 7. An executioner; 8. A bird-catcher; 9. One who uses double-tongued speech (slander);
10. A jailer; 11. One who recites spells to subdue dragons. [From] the Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya.

There are fourteen types of existence: sheep-butcher, pig-breeder, bird-catcher, fisherman, deer-hunter, rabbit-trapper, robber, executioner, ox-slayer, elephant-binder, *dāna*-practitioner who curses dragons, jailer, slanderer, and those who delight in causing harm.
These are correctly termed "mental intentions that are broad and heavy, whose harmfulness is truly profound. *Ji* (豕) also means to capture; it may also be written as *yu* (漁).
Question: Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "furthermore, by drawing near" to "having no expectations," what is its meaning? Answer:

As stated in the Mahā-sūtra, a Bodhisattva fears the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) as one who cherishes their own life. And as stated in the *Sūtra of the Questions of the Devaputra Śāntamati*, the Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Suppose there were someone suffering from hunger and thirst and emaciated; would they rather endure that hunger and thirst than eat food mixed with poison?"
The food of a bodhisattva is also like this: one who is stingy, envious, immoral, harsh-spoken, lazy, distracted, or ignorant will never seek the fruit of the stage of the two vehicles.

The Buddha told the devaputra: "Just as a poor man’s food is poisonous for a wheel-turning monarch, so too are the precepts and diligence of those in the two vehicles like the breaking of precepts and laziness for a bodhisattva; therefore, they do not approach him."

Regarding the teaching that one does not wish to be intimate with narrow-mindedness, nor seek gain, offerings, or honor—this present sutra states that such a person is neither criticized nor disparaged, nor is he excluded from communal residence, nor is he abandoned; rather, his virtues are not praised and his faults are not spoken of.

Thus, we know that this is in every respect different from that [other] teaching. Furthermore, because it is taught that both of these two vehicles shall ultimately attain Buddhahood, they are not [the same].
What benefit is there in citing those who, like the followers of the *Kṣayamukha-sūtra*, are people who do not understand?

Question: From the passage concerning Mañjuśrī in the sutra down to the phrase "regarding those with whom one is intimate," what is the meaning? Answer: There are two reasons: first, the condition of prolonged defilement;
second, the condition of being an unsuitable vessel. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "It is, for example, like cooked food that all people love to eat."
Women are likewise thus; because they cause men to become attached and unable to let go, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* says:
"A pure breeze has no form, yet it can still be grasped; a venomous snake contains poison, yet it can still be touched; but the heart of a woman is difficult to approach.

It is like pointing a sword at an enemy—one might still prevail—but the female thief who harms people is difficult to restrain. The *Caturvarga-vinaya* states that frequenting the homes of laypeople [leads to such consequences].
The five transgressions are: first, frequently seeing women; second, frequently associating with them; third, increasingly intimate association; fourth, the arising of lustful thoughts;

and fifth, sometimes leading to death or, next, the suffering of near-death. Now, it may be argued that while the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles regarding what is prohibited is acceptable, one must distinguish between the underlying intent of the two teachings:
the Small Vehicle is for one's own cultivation, whereas this [Great Vehicle] is for the propagation of the sutras and the fulfillment of the Small Vehicle.
This is for the purpose of abandoning minor [faults] while that is solely for the purpose of prohibiting [certain actions] without providing exceptions;
this prevents transgressions and promotes benefit. Question: From "not entering another's house alone" up to "not being pleased with having the same teacher," what is the reason?

Answer: There are three reasons: first, the condition of censure; second, the condition of improper conduct; and third, the condition of distraction. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that one should avoid ten [such things].

The four defilements, the storehouse of karma, the concealment of the six directions, the distancing from the four evil friends, and the embracing of the four virtuous friends—these are called the fourteen.

As the *Dīrgha Āgama* states, there are four types of evil karma of body and speech, namely: sexual misconduct, killing, stealing, and lying. There are four evil causes, namely: greed, hatred, delusion, and pride.

One should avoid the six ways of wasting wealth and the Dharma: first, indulgence in alcohol; second, gambling; third, dissipation; fourth, attachment to the arts [of performance]; [fifth, addiction to women; sixth, addiction to food].

"Delighting in the five evil friends, mutually harming one another, and gradually following their teachings"—this is now said to be a constant admonition regarding the practice of *sukhavihāra* (peaceful conduct), yet its description is far too coarse.
How could one who practices *sukhavihāra* indulge in wine or gambling? As for "concealing the six directions," as stated in the *Dīrgha Āgama*:
"In the city of Rājagṛha, there was the son of an elder named Sujāta, whose lineage had been established for generations. Every morning..."

He practiced the ritual of the six directions so that the six deities might constantly protect him. After his father’s death, he suddenly encountered the Buddha and asked whether there were any teachings on the principles of Dharma.
The Buddha said, "There are. Your father is the eastern direction; your teachers are the southern direction; your wife and children are the western direction;
your relatives and friends are the northern direction; your servants are the downward direction; and śramaṇas of high virtue are the upward direction. Now...

For a beginner who propagates the sutras, it is not permitted to associate with such [people]; how then could one encounter the Buddha’s True Dharma through the heterodox calculations of the secular world?
Furthermore, even the four types of evil friends and the four types of virtuous friends are not things that those practicing for peace and bliss should avoid.
It is further said: *huài* (膾) means to mince; to cut finely is to make minced meat (*huài*). *Xuàn* (衒) means to go about selling, or to advertise oneself. *Lǐ* (里) refers to a neighborhood.

Five households constitute a neighborhood (*kula*), five neighborhoods constitute a village (*grāma*), and twenty-five households constitute a residential quarter (*vīthi*). This refers to dwelling within the confines of a single village-quarter.

Regarding the methods of begging for alms, there are thirteen types: first, abiding in right precepts; second, abiding in right deportment; third, abiding in right livelihood; fourth, abiding in right view; fifth, relying on the proper occasion;

sixth, relying on the proper time; seventh, relying on the proper place; eighth, relying on the proper sequence; ninth, relying on the proper manner; tenth, relying on the proper measure; eleventh, relying on the proper recipient; twelfth, relying on the proper vessel; and thirteenth, relying on the proper distribution.
Nine, freedom from greed; ten, freedom from grasping and attachment; eleven, freedom from anger and vexation; twelve, freedom from coarseness and rudeness; thirteen, freedom from arrogance.

The first four concern dwelling correctly in begging; the next four concern dwelling in the rules of conduct; the final five concern abandoning afflictions. Furthermore, there are two kinds [of abandonment]:
first, for one's own benefit; second, for the benefit of others. From the *Twentyfold Jewel Garland Sūtra* (*Viṃśatikā-ratnamegha-sūtra*), after obtaining alms-food, it is to be divided.

Divide the meal into four parts: one part to offer to fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*), one part intended for the poor and lowly beggars, one part to bestow upon sentient beings of water and land, and one part for oneself to eat.

Now, regarding the thirteen [precepts], it is said that while the first eight may be observed, the latter five are minor rules (*kṣudraka-dharma*) which the practitioner of *anurakṣaṇādharma* does not employ.

There is a profound and subtle practice of contemplation that is inherently free from attachment; it is a practice of "leaving" while not actually leaving [the world], as practiced when begging for food.
The method for begging for food, which possesses the three virtues, is explained in detail in the ancient commentaries on Śāriputra and Śākya-Śāṇavāsī.
Question: Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "robes and bedding" to "providing offerings for peace and happiness," what is its meaning?
Answer: As stated following the verses on the four types of Dharma-preachers in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it says: "One may enter a sandalwood forest yet take away only stinking leaves;
one may enter a mountain of seven treasures yet seek only crystal. Likewise, there are those who enter the Buddha-dharma but do not take up the bliss of Nirvāṇa, instead seeking [other things].

To seek gain through offerings is to deceive oneself and others alike; this current teaching is intended as a warning for those who crave fame and profit, not as a prohibition against those practicing for the sake of peace and happiness.
For such practitioners already possess the great benefit of peace and happiness themselves;
it is only out of concern that those who propagate the sutras might encounter conditions for regression that this [prohibition] was established.

Question: What is meant by the majesty of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*)? Answer: There are four types of Wheel-Turning Kings. When the Golden Wheel encounters them, they submit at the mere sight of its splendor;

the Silver Wheel brings them down by dispatching an envoy; the Copper Wheel brings them to submission by manifesting its majestic power; and the Iron Wheel brings them down only when the spear is raised.

These are to be correlated respectively with the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the Self-enjoyment-body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*), the Other-enjoyment-body (*parasaṃbhogakāya*), and the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Here, it refers to the Transformation-body transforming those of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

Since humans are [governed by] the iron wheel, why does the treatise (śāstra) list all three bodies? If this sutra only transforms those of the two vehicles, yet the treatise lists them all, then the treatise would be in error.
Furthermore, if one uses the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) to transform those of the two vehicles, why then say it "destroys the demon of changeable existence" (vaśavartin-māra)?
Moreover, how could the characteristics of liberation (vimukti-lakṣaṇa) and the characteristics of emerging from the earth be so fundamentally contradictory?
Question: What is the intent behind the title "Chapter on the Arising of Joy"? Answer: There are three points within the text.

This chapter specifically clarifies the lifespan and the distinct merits of those who propagate the *Anrakugyō* (Peaceful Practices); it arises sequentially to resolve these doubts and to give rise to sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).

Furthermore, the merit of the Dharma-preacher is clarified; the merit obtained by those who assist in the correct teaching, rely upon it, and propagate the *Anraku-gyō* (Peaceful Conduct) is explained.

By means of the "Never-Disparaging" [chapter], the Buddha himself is shown to have previously dwelt in the stage of a causal practitioner (*hetu-bhūmi*), propagating this sutra through peaceful conduct, patience, and so forth, thereby exhorting beings to practice and study it; hence this chapter follows. Now, the "Life Span" and "Distinction" [chapters] are discussed.

Because the merit [of the teaching] resolves doubts, it is appropriate that he comes by means of a miraculous manifestation (*abhinirhāra*). If this is so, why do the "Expedient Means" chapter and others also testify that Maitreya comes because of doubt?
For what reason? After Mañjuśrī has finished answering, one fears that [doubt] might arise; how could this prove that the propagation of the sutra is not in vain?
It must be understood that the purpose of summoning those below is fundamentally to give rise to doubt, and that doubt constitutes the primary point.
This is what is meant by that. Question:

What does the treatise say? Answer: The treatise states: "Seventh, because the teaching and transformation of sentient beings is unsurpassed, immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas emerge from the earth.
Now, it is said that this commentary is most appropriate, as it correctly clarifies the Tathāgata’s dwelling in his former abodes.

Since those transformed and the transformed have long been numerous in their retinues, and those who receive the Dharma are no small recipients whose merit is great, [the Buddha] summons the distant past to manifest the near and causes them to propagate the Sūtra to benefit those currently being transformed; there is nothing superior to this, hence it is called "unsurpassed.

Why need one laboriously speak of "practicing for the sake of peaceful bliss" or "arising from causes," and so forth? If that were the case, then [the Bodhisattvas] should have leaped forth without [the need for] peaceful bliss.

The respondent said: "If one follows the general principle (*sāmānya*), there is a basis; yet if one distinguishes specifically (*viśeṣa*), it is not so. The fruit of peace and bliss pervades its practice, and that practice is likewise universal. Now, we follow from the beginning.

Since the beginning proceeds from the specific, and the fruit is universal while the cause is specific, how could one who has reached the ultimate end be made to perform practices from the beginning again?
Therefore, we know this is the practice of cultivating the principle and propagating the sutra. The principle is itself the three virtues (*triguṇa*)."
It is said that Nirvana is identical to the "Chapter on the Threefold Dharma-Maintenance" and the "Donning of Armor" of the Dharma Master;
from the time of the Dharma Master onward, all have established practice based upon principle to propagate the Great Dharma.
Thus, each of those Bodhisattvas is a leader of the exhortation, abiding in the ultimate three virtues while propagating the wondrous teachings of the three guidelines.

Question: Regarding this "Chapter on the Leaping Up" (*Ullambana-parivarta*), does the character for "leap" (*ullambana*) also imply being barefoot? Answer: If one were to interpret it as leaping in this manner, it would indeed carry the sense of being barefoot;
this is like water overflowing, which should be understood as arising from the water. However, I say that it need not necessarily be so.

What is meant by "leaping" is simply a surging upward, just as Śāriputra’s mind was filled with joy and surged upward as described above. Why must it necessarily carry the meaning of being barefoot? At first glance...
It may be slightly like water leaping up for that reason.
Question: Someone has previously asked why it is not said they come from the side, but rather that they leap forth. Answer:
This clarifies that by relying on the four practices to uphold the sutra, they leap forth from the realm of birth and death; now, it is asked whether each of these bodhisattvas...

These leaders of the assembly each headed sixty thousand followers; their bodies were all golden in color and possessed the thirty-two marks, and they resided in the stage of the "Successor" (Upapadya).

Since they had already transcended the realm of birth and death, they should not be practicing the conduct of beginners. If they had already transcended the realm of birth and death, why did they dwell in the lower regions?
When questions regarding phenomena and principles do not accord with the underlying meaning, at what time should these four practices be cultivated?
Now, as one practices, one is finally emerging from the realm of birth and death.
Question: Why does the Buddha, at that time, speak extensively on this sutra? Answer: It is to manifest the merit of the Buddha’s transformation of others;

it merely stops them [from wrongdoing] and does not permit negligence, yet even if they were to protect themselves [from such negligence], what fault would there be? Now, it is said that there is no lack of reason for making this statement.

The first obstacle is not knowing the lifespan [of the Buddha], for which the earth’s quaking serves as the introduction, while simultaneously causing the earth to quake so that the sutra may be propagated extensively.
The second is not knowing the scope of the transformation, as it distinguishes the specific locations where the teaching is propagated according to conditions.
Question: Regarding the passage in the sutra from "all bodhisattvas" up to "as if for half a day," what does this mean?

Answer: The *kalpas* described in this sutra may be reckoned in terms of days and nights, months, seasons, or years. Here, they are calculated by combining days and nights; thus, twenty-five nights do not fail to constitute fifty minor *kalpas*.
Alternatively, they may be fifty days, fifty months, or even seasons and years, so that the praise of their virtues becomes ever more profound.

At that time, the duration was such that all could perceive it; his power of spiritual transformation (*ṛddhi*) was equal to the duration of the praise. Through the power of his spiritual transformations, he altered their original minds, and through his holy supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), he extended or shortened the passage of time.
Sentient beings received the Dharma and thereby forgot their fatigue; how much more so when the Sages bestow their hidden grace (*adhiṣṭhāna*)—who would then give rise to weariness or distaste?
Therefore, the fourfold assembly thought it was but the time of a meal, yet sustained by the nourishment of the Dharma-food and governed by his supernormal powers, many kalpas passed.
If one’s lifespan is not diminished, why is it now said to be merely fifty days and nights? Or when it is said to be "a year" and so forth—as in the case of a mere meal—what is the harm?
Why must one speak of *kalpas* to confuse [the matter]? It is a laborious and circuitous attempt at forced interpretation.
Is the Buddha’s power of wisdom and supernormal faculties exhausted that he cannot cause fifty small *kalpas* to pass like the duration of a meal?
Furthermore, why not simply say "fifty kalpas" instead of saying "small [kalpas]"? In that case, one should likewise speak of "small nights," "small times," "small years," and "small months.

If this were so, what would constitute a "great day," a "great night," a "great time," a "great year," or a "great month"? If a single small unit—such as a night—is taken to be a kalpa, then what further need is there for [the concept of] great units?

For every great unit corresponds to eighty small units; thus, one great increase-and-decrease cycle constitutes one small [kalpa]. If a mere night and so forth were considered a kalpa, why would there be a need for these further distinctions?

Regarding the discourse on the prolongation and contraction of the lifespan of noble beings through the transformation of the mind, although such treatises generally clarify the nature of time and so forth, this passage cites the general to imply the specific.

Furthermore, if one were to name the *kalpa* as "pure," then within the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, it should simply state that seven *kalpas* constitute one [pure] *kalpa*, or that one *kalpa* constitutes seven [ordinary] *kalpas*.
Is it then by means of the seven days that one compares them to a single *kalpa* to demonstrate prolongation and contraction? This is according to various sūtras and śāstras.
However, since both the extension and the contraction of time are equal in duration—both being kalpas—is it only within this [intermediate period] that they occur?
Therefore, this interpretation cannot be trusted.
Question: From the passage in the Sūtra beginning with "I, among this assembly... up to "resolving the doubts of the assembly," what is the meaning? Answer: This is not understood.
Now, one asks: why does Śākyamuni, as the successor (kṣetra-parigraha), not recognize those who practice the four modes of peaceful conduct?
One should reply: "Ajita" is a corruption of "Aśvita. Furthermore, one asks:
why does the sutra state that from the Sahā world-system up to all [beings] shall attain Buddhahood? One answers: it is to manifest the wisdom of their dwelling place.

Only by being profoundly aware of this site of transformation at Gayā does one know that the previous transformation was not this present Gayā; thus it is said that [the Buddha] "always dwells on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa" and so forth.
Now, since this is not the present transformation, at what time were these four practices of peaceful dwelling (catur-āśvāsa-caryā) actually performed?

Furthermore, because the location differs and the wisdom is profound, these four practices do not constitute a teaching for this assembly. Moreover, after the kalpa has been destroyed, Gayā should be changed; even if...
If every eon is named Gayā, then while the names are identical, their substances must necessarily be distinct. How, then, can it be said, "I am always here"?
Furthermore, is the Gayā that is eternally present the same as or different from the Gayā that undergoes formation and destruction? Is that which is neither formed nor destroyed called Gayā?
Or is that which is neither formed nor destroyed called the Flower Treasury (Kusumatalagarbha)? Is it not the case that what does not abide is called the Flower Treasury?
"Is it not the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya)? He replied, "The Buddha was born in Gayā and attained enlightenment in Magadha; since the distance between them is not great, it is said to be 'not far.
Question: Regarding the statement in the Sūtra, 'From this point until now, more than forty years have passed,' what does this mean? Answer: It is according to the original cause."
The *Pratyaya-sūtra* states that he left home at nineteen; the *Asaṃjñika-samādhi-sūtra* states that he attained enlightenment at thirty.

According to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, when the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he told Subhadra: "I left home at nineteen, and after leaving home, fifty years passed before I spoke of the time of my attaining enlightenment.
This would mean the Buddha was eighty years old. Some, however, say he was nineteen [at his death].
Five years after his renunciation, he served the sages; six years of asceticism followed, and at thirty, he attained enlightenment.
Thus, he told Subhadra that fifty years had passed; therefore, when it is now said to be "over forty years," this refers to over seventy.
Furthermore, various Mahāyāna sūtras state that he renounced the world at twenty-nine and attained enlightenment at thirty-five. Additionally, the *Ekottarika Āgama* contains miscellaneous accounts.
The *Chuyao jing* (Udānavarga), the *Heshumilun* (Mahīśāsaka-vinaya), and the *Beihua jing* (Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra) all state [the Buddha’s age] as twenty-nine;

the *Shanjianlun* (Samantapāsādikā) states it as thirty-five. The *Chengdao benqi jing* (Lalitavistara-sūtra) says that at the time of his renunciation, he pointed to Yaśodharā’s womb and said, "Six years hence, you shall give birth to a son.
Subsequently, she conceived Rāhula; it was on the night the Buddha attained enlightenment after six years of asceticism that Rāhula was born.
It is said that he remained in the womb for six years, but it is not stated that he remained in the womb for eleven years;

therefore, we know he left home at twenty-nine and attained enlightenment at thirty-five. Within those six years, he performed ascetic practices. The master Bodhiruci, citing a verse from a sutra, says:
"Eight years as an infant, seven years as a youth, four years studying the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), and ten years receiving [instruction]."
He spent six years among the five desires, practiced asceticism for six years, attained enlightenment at thirty-five, and taught all sentient beings for forty-five years.
Both the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* and the *Record of the Western Regions* state that he left home at twenty-nine and attained enlightenment at thirty-five.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* says the Buddha’s lifespan was eighty years; thus, if one says "more than forty years," it refers to seventy-five years. And so forth.
The year of his initial attainment of enlightenment was forty-one years ago; thus, having passed the age of forty, he is now said to be "over forty.

However, as for the Buddha’s time of birth, the location of his parinirvāṇa, his physical marks, and his preaching of the Dharma, the various schools differ because they perceive these matters differently; there is no need for a definitive judgment.

This is precisely why the ancient masters, in their exegesis of the sūtras, added the categories of the "gradual" (*anupūrva*) and the "indeterminate-secret" (*aniyata-guhyaka*). Were it not for this, [the distinctions would not hold].
How can one definitively judge that the *Mahāvastu* and other such scriptures are not authentic? Nor should one take the fact that a teaching is mentioned many times as proof that it is definitive.

If being mentioned frequently were the criterion for authenticity, then the Sthavira school itself would not be considered authentic; how much more so when there are various differences, all of which are the Buddha’s teachings?
This is what is meant by the saying: "They heard the same thing, yet their interpretations differed."
Question: From the passage beginning with "For example" up to "difficult to believe," what is the meaning? Answer: The examples are cited because they are difficult to believe.

The beauty of the color is a metaphor for the Buddha’s marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) which adorn him; his black hair signifies that although the Buddha is eighty years old, he lacks the appearance of aging.

This is because at all times he is excellent as he traverses his former haunts. Thus, it is said in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* among the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) that he possesses "perpetual youth."
Now, Elder, you ask: "If these bodhisattvas also possess the thirty-two marks, they must necessarily have the eighty minor characteristics (*anuvyañjana*).
Why did you previously state, Elder, that one should practice the 'Practice of Peaceful Dwelling' (*sukhavihāra*), for peace (*sukha*) is named *nirvāṇa*, and in *nirvāṇa* there is no aging?
Furthermore, the seventh sutra states: "One who can uphold this sutra does not age and does not die. This would then contradict the analogy; the analogy of the dharma would be rendered untenable.

The two elders are in opposition, and the two youths are at variance with one another. Furthermore, it is said that "two fives" represent the Buddha's emergence from birth and death, signifying that he does not dwell within the twenty-five realms of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
Now, I say that these various bodhisattvas, having emerged from the earth, immediately proceed to empty space;

this too signifies that they do not dwell within the twenty-five realms of existence. Why, then, is this compared to a hundred-year-old man? Moreover, it is said that what precedes represents the Buddha.
It has been nearly eighty years since his attainment of the Way, yet he appears as if only twenty-five; how then can these various bodhisattvas be considered like old men?
Moreover, the principle of merely stating that they have "emerged from the twenty-five states of existence" remains unestablished.

Question: Why does the Sūtra refer to a person who is one hundred years old? Answer: It is to indicate that the bodhisattvas being transformed [by the Buddha] occupy a high and distant station, adorned with a hundred merits.
[The Buddha] says, "I have nurtured them so that their Way may flourish. This matter is difficult to believe;
yet now it is said that the Buddha’s body is likewise adorned with a hundred merits, and his virtue and status are likewise high and distant. If a [bodhisattva] were to surpass the Buddha...
[Question: Why is it that while the stage of a Bodhisattva (*bodhisattva-avasthā*) is high, they cause those who have just begun their practice to attain peace and happiness?

[Question: Regarding the Sūtra passage from "The Buddha is also like this" up to "it is extremely rare," what is its meaning? [Answer: First, it restates the brevity of the time when the Buddha attained enlightenment;
subsequently, it clarifies the seven virtues of a Bodhisattva. As for these seven virtues: first, the duration of cultivation is long; second, the exertion is diligent.

[The Buddha] has progressed through the three concentrations with mastery, attained the supernormal powers, practiced for a long time, is able to cultivate the Dharma, and is skillful in questioning and answering.
Since he now possesses these seven virtues, why does he admonish him not to drink alcohol, gamble, keep livestock, and so forth,
as well as to stay away from eunuchs and executioners?
Question: Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "For example, like a young man" up to "that which the whole world does not believe," what is its meaning?
Answer: This serves to mutually illuminate the prose section. The father’s words describe the signs of youthfulness—handsome appearance, black hair, and the fullness of his features;

the son’s response describes the signs of long cultivation yet still lacking perfection—white hair, a wrinkled face, and so forth. That his hair has turned white indicates that he has long cultivated the Noble Path.

The wrinkled face and furrowed brow are signs that his physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*) were not yet fully perfected; "not yet perfected" here refers to youth, whereas the *Nānyabala* says it refers to old age.

"Wandering through the old" refers to old age, whereas the *Nānyabala* says it refers to youth. Thus we know that the Buddha manifested a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) to establish a teaching for the sake of manifestation, representing the years when the complexion is beautiful and the hair is black;
whereas the Bodhisattva abides in the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) to receive the Dharma, representing the years of advanced age with a wrinkled face.
The signs of this are such that one looks toward transformation and its retribution, yet the marks are not yet perfected;

because the causes of delusion are not severed and practice during cultivation is deficient, these bodhisattvas, though their seven virtues are already perfected, look toward those four stages. Thus, being like a father who has practiced for a long time yet is surpassed by a son, the situation is precisely analogous.
Question: What is the purpose of this inquiry? Answer: Here, the great assembly, having seen that the Bodhisattva’s rank is high and his retinue vast, gives rise to doubt.

Now, it is clarified that while the Dharmakāya is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha has recently attained realization, whereas the Saṃbhogakāya has long since been certified; thus, [the Buddha] transforms these members of the assembly.
What is there to doubt? Therefore, this chapter follows the preceding one. Now, it is asked: for whom does this chapter appear, and why does it come? [The answer is:
because those who increase their path and diminish their births all regress from the Mahāyāna; thus we know that it cannot simply be called the "present reward-body" (*sambhogakāya*).

One should rather say it is the "Dharma-body realized over a long duration. Therefore, when the treatise lists the reward-body, it immediately cites the "Life Span" chapter of the sūtra as its scriptural authority.
Because this is established by realization, one cannot say it refers only to "today. If one speaks of only the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*, what sutra lacks such a teaching?
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says, "Vairocana," and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says, "The Buddha-body is precisely the *dharmakāya*," and further states, "the adamantine body.
Other scriptures state, "The Buddha’s true *dharmakāya* is like empty space," and so forth. Such examples regarding the *prajñāpāramitā* of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) are exceedingly numerous.

Why not first resolve the doubt regarding the earth’s quaking so that the assembly hearing the Dharma may recognize it as a true transformation? Why do all those who have distinguished their merits not appear here?
Why is the merit accumulated over such a long period obscured by suffering, such that one merely says this chapter "resolves doubts" and thus comes to believe the discourse on the distant past?
That which was concealed throughout the entire dispensation is only now revealed in this chapter; how can it be said that the near-perfection [of the Buddha's life] is explained within this section?

Although there are statements regarding long-term realization, one does not recognize the underlying intention behind the discourse on "distance. Furthermore, the commentary on the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits" also states:
"Having heard the benefit of the Buddha’s lifespan being long and distant, one fails to realize it face-to-face; the merit of speaking of 'distance' is profound.
Why does it not simply say "hearing the benefit of the Buddha’s Dharma-body being empty and quiescent," rather than saying "hearing the benefit of its being long and distant"?

Furthermore, it is said that if the nineteen chapters constitute the main body of the teaching, the final five chapters clarify the fruit of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), which is further divided into two parts:

the first two chapters clarify the fruit already perfected, while the latter three chapters clarify the fruit not yet perfected. Within the section on the fruit already perfected, there are again two parts:
first, the formal clarification of perfection; second, the identification of the assembly at that time and how their realizations differed accordingly. Now, [the author] says:

The two meanings of "circulation" (*pravartana*) and "correctness" (*samyaktva*) are fundamentally distinct; how could they be divided into two sections? Furthermore, these two meanings are mutually contradictory.

Moreover, regarding the attainment of the fruit through the three cycles of teaching, the perfection of the fruit is fully explained at the beginning of the "Expedient Means" (*Upāya-paṛiccheda*) chapter: the wisdom of the fruit is identical to the meaning of the fulfillment of the fruit throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
The elder’s old age is a direct metaphor for the fruit; on the day he lost his son, that fruit was already [present].

When the *Yāksa-vidyā-siddhi-mudrā* was composed, the title "Teacher of the City of Transformation" (the *tathāgatagarbha*) was already long perfected as the fruit of wisdom; thus, it is surely one who has realized the fruit.
By revealing the "robe and jewel" within the five hundred [disciples], it clarifies that they were not merely friends on the path of causes.

Since the meaning of the fruit has already been unfolded by opening the topknot of the Wheel-Turning King, the discourse on the "Life Span" (*āyus-pramāṇa*) is established to manifest the proximity of the ancient fruit, thereby making known that those transformed by the ancient fruit are none other than these.

It is difficult to fathom how long it will take before they become spiritual kin; to speak much at random without understanding the essential meaning is futile. The *Nanwen lun* (Treatise on Questions from the South) states:

"To treat those of the seventh [stage] who lack merit and do not accumulate roots of goodness in the First Vehicle, one explains the First Vehicle, yet they do not accept it as the first but rather as the seventh.

To counter this, the analogy of the physician is taught. Furthermore, the *Lun* (Treatise) says: [The text continues: ...Furthermore, the *Lun* says: "Furthermore, the *Lun* says... (Note: The provided source text appears to repeat the phrase "The *Lun* says" at the end).
Regarding the seventh person: because their faculties (*indriya*) are not yet matured, [the Buddha] manifests the measure of *nirvāṇa* in order to bring them to maturity.

The commentary explains: those who have not yet accumulated roots of goodness in the present are called "those with immature faculties. To cause them to accumulate roots of goodness, one causes them to aspire for and grasp the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), manifesting a limited duration of *nirvāṇa*.
This is called the "measure" (*mātra*). Only after they have accumulated roots of goodness will they subsequently be tamed and matured. Now, according to this treatise...

Since the text lacks words that resolve doubts and contains no expressions that provoke such doubts, and since the ultimate fruit has long been established without reference to the present, if it were merely to refer to the present—given that the present fruit has already been discussed—why would it need to emerge so abruptly to resolve doubts regarding the fruit?

Furthermore, if it were simply to distinguish the fruit in contrast to the cause, what is so extraordinary about this, as it is constantly discussed in the various sutras? Why then should the number of *bodhisattvas* on the path increase and those in the stage of *śrāvaka* decrease by several times over?

In the remaining generations, there has never been such an experience; people’s sentiments all secretly agree that since the text states they were "not yet mature," one knows for certain that the meanings of the Trace and the Origin are distinct.

How could there be a skillful means that reveals the provisional while still being called "the arising of the capacity" within the section on the Propagation of the Teaching after the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs?

Thus we know that while the Trace is mature, the Origin must be heard as "arising" [only] through the long and distant [period]; this is why, even though one understands the Trace, [one still requires the revelation of the Origin].

Because it reveals that those who have not attained realization [of the truth] have long since entered the One Vehicle, it manifests the original ground to benefit sentient beings, causing them to know that his merits were perfected and matured from the beginning.

He repeatedly manifests birth and nirvana in countless ways; because he is neither one nor many, he manifests extinction as non-extinction, and because he manifests birth as non-birth, he has truly been perfected since time immemorial, yet manifests birth and extinction for the sake of sentient beings.
Regarding the initial manifestation of the knowledge that birth is non-birth, the teachings throughout the entire dispensation all state that it was first perfected and long expounded;

this is indeed not an easy matter. Since those of the past and present have been lost in the confusion of the ford, the *Treatise* states: "Eighth, the manifestation of attaining great bodhi because it is unsurpassed.
Because this chapter has appeared to manifest the three kinds of Buddha-bodhi, we know that the intent of the *Treatise* is to comprehensively clarify what is personally realized.

Taking the wisdom that accords with the Buddha’s Bodhi as the retribution for retribution, and taking the Dharma that accords with the Buddha’s Bodhi as the Dharma, [we see that] the present *nirmāṇakāya* (manifestation body) and those of the intermediate period—whether proclaiming birth or proclaiming extinction—all belong to the *nirmāṇabuddha-bodhi*.

Therefore, the *svasaṃbhogakāya* (self-enjoyment body) is invariably remote, while within this context, the *nirmāṇakāya* is invariably proximate. Furthermore, the *parasaṃbhogakāya* (other-enjoyment body) is not fixed as being either near or far.

If the fulfillment [of the vows] were truly achieved in this present life, then one would personally enjoy the fruit without need for distant discourse; yet if it were truly accomplished over a long duration, the matter must be explained according to reality.

In that case, the retribution of personal enjoyment would not be simultaneous with the long period of time. How could it be as in the case of Śākyamuni, where all are metaphorically compared to this dust-mote world?
While the treatise is concise and speaks directly of the three bodies (*trikāya*) in terms of their long-term duration, it fully points to the original sūtras and commentaries.
To explain this: both the distant and the near traditions discuss the person who is fully endowed with the three bodies (trikāya), yet they do not perceive it.

They merely say that if the three bodies of the fruit are truly near, they are not distant fruits; and if the three bodies of the distant fruit are truly remote, they are not near. Now, by pointing to the near to reveal the distant, we see that the three bodies are inherently present.
Because they are distant, we know that the provisional scriptures all manifest the three bodies as near. If one does not realize the near, how can one recognize the distant?
Therefore, it is not for nothing that the affairs of a single lifetime are not understood; they are now being revealed, yet they are truly not easy to know.

However, whether near or far, in terms of phenomena and principle, there is no fundamental basis. Now, even "the present" should not be restricted to a specific time; how could the Dharmakāya and Saṃbhogakāya be confined solely to the distant or the near?

Thus we know that the *Śāstra* says, "The attainment of the unsurpassed path" means that within the process of accomplishment, the ultimate is manifested; therefore, it is called "unsurpassed. (Thus ends the third section of the *Śāstra*).
The meaning of "Buddha" encompasses both the fundamental and the present; furthermore, the treatise states that the ninth [attribute] is the manifestation of unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.

It explains this by means of the analogy of a physician. Regarding the use of the physician analogy among the seven types of pride (*māna*): it is taught to transform those whose faculties (*indriya*) are not yet mature, manifesting entry into extinction so as to bring their faculties to maturity.

When the Buddha enters *nirvāṇa*, his transformative activity ceases, yet this is not a cessation like that of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*); therefore, it is called "unsurpassed."

Now, it is said that this is cessation in the intermediate state, not cessation in the ear; since it has not yet ceased, to speak of "cessation" is like a metaphorical transformation-cessation (*nirmāṇa-nirodha*) rather than true cessation.
Therefore, within the teachings of a single lifetime, it was not taught that there was ever a place where [cessation] had previously been established—what cessation could there be?
Since it is absent from all the sūtras, it is called "unexcelled. Thus, we know that the intent of the treatise deeply accords with the core tenets of the sūtras; it is merely a matter of time.

To explain this on behalf of others: it contradicts the intent of the teaching. Furthermore, in the previous explanation of the *nidāna* (preface) of the sutra, it was stated that "this chapter is in response to Maitreya’s request.
Now, that which constitutes a response to a request consists solely of the circulation of the authentic scripture; it does not refer to merely making a vow to propagate the Dharma.

If one were to take the response to Śāriputra’s request as a precedent, that might indeed be acceptable; however, the meanings of "original" (*hon*) and "traced" (*shaku*) are fundamentally distinct—how can this be so?
It must be explained separately. Question:
What is the meaning of the title of this chapter, "The Tathāgata"? Answer: "Tathāgata" is the general name for the Dharma-body, Reward-body, Response-body, and Transformation-body.

"Life-span" (*āyus*) refers to the measure of life received by a sentient being, which implies a specific limit; therefore, this chapter clarifies the essential nature of the life-span of these three types of Buddha-bodies.

The principle of the *dharmatā* abiding within its limits is revealed so as to respond to the capacities of all beings; this is the *saṃbhogakāya*. Now, if one explains this chapter based on the three bodies (*trikāya*), it accords with the *Śāstra* and harmonizes with the *Sūtra*.

Why begrudge a vertical discussion that clarifies and evaluates the fundamental and the manifested? Furthermore, regarding the term "measure" (*shòuliàng*) in the phrase "measuring the lifespan" (*shòuliàng*), the character for "lifespan" (*shòu*) is pronounced in the rising tone (*shēngdì*), while the character for "measure" (*liàng*) is pronounced in the level tone (*píngdì*).

This refers to the devaluation and evaluation, the calculation and comparison, of the lifespans of the three Buddhas—namely, the disparagement and praise, and the reckoning and assessment of the three Buddhas' longevity.
Master Shou now explains that "depreciation" (bian) means to retreat, to diminish, to reduce, or to detract; whereas "praise" (bao) means to take up, to initiate, and is also termed "eulogy.

Therefore, regarding the longevity of the three Buddhas, though their lifespans are extolled over long kalpas, one has not yet attained even a hair’s breadth or a single thought-moment by which to depreciate and measure their faults.
Furthermore, the *Dhāraṇī* does not speak of whether there is a limit or no limit, nor of length, shortness, sameness, or difference; it speaks only of praise and depreciation, gain and loss.

Thus, it follows that the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) is subject to an end, whereas the *dharmakāya* (dharma-body) and *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) are not so; for while the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* are immeasurable, the *nirmāṇakāya* is not.

Therefore, one should know that the text of this chapter discusses vertically the long duration of the lives of the three Buddhas of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), as well as the similarities and differences between them and the three Buddhas of the provisional traces (*traces-Buddhas*). This is fully explained according to the commentaries of the ancient masters on the titles of the chapters.
Question: Why is it that one does not use "Physician" as the title for this chapter, but instead names it "Life Span"?

Answer: Because by citing the "Life Span," the analogy of the physician is set aside; we follow the primary over the secondary. Here, "Life Span" is the dharma (the subject), while "physician" is the metaphor (the illustration).
We cite the dharma to encompass the metaphor; it is not a matter of primary and secondary.

Question: Furthermore, there is a question stating that since the initial outline of the text says, "First, the lifespan is presented, excluding those whose faculties are not yet mature," why is this not the main body (*dharmakāya*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, but rather categorized as part of the dissemination section (*parivarta*)? Answer: It is because the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) intended for the primary audience was specifically suited for the Śrāvakas;
it was shown to transform those with initially immature faculties after [the Buddha’s] passing. Therefore, although it was taught, it is not the main body.

The fact that the lifespan [of the Buddha] was not recorded for the śrāvakas, and that even though he is described as a physician, no small matter was recorded for them—considering that Jñānakośa requested to return earlier than this, it would not be so if he had requested to return midway;

why then did he return so quickly? For these reasons, one might object that this chapter is merely a dissemination (*pravartana*) and not the main body (*samyak-artha*), which would present a contradiction.
Now, we say: since the non-accumulation of merit has already been discussed as previously stated, it must logically belong to the main body.
How could one wait for a definitive argument to know that this master, fearing the instability of his own doctrine, merely raised this question to block the doubts of others?

It is a futile application of reasoning from the outset that ultimately lacks any standard. If you claim that because the Śrāvakas are not recorded [in their full lifespans], they do not belong to the primary category, we shall now counter-argue:

since their original lifespans have not been revealed, they should not be included as part of the primary group. This is truly because you fail to understand the two gates of the fundamental and the trace, which has led to this result.
Regarding the judgment of the advancement and retreat of the texts: the Fundamental Gate (Honmon) is fundamentally and eternally distinct from all other teachings of the Trace Gate (Jikimon).
Because the Trace Gate may possess both differences and similarities, when viewed from the perspective of the present within the Trace Gate, the present is primary and the past is secondary;

yet when the Fundamental Gate is viewed in relation to the Trace, the fundamental is primary and the trace is secondary. Both gates—secondary and primary—are equally termed "primary," and only beyond these two primary aspects does the Propagation (Ryūtsū) truly reside.

Therefore, within this single sutra, the fundamental [nature] is taken as primary; when the [Buddha’s] traces had not yet been revealed, Gaya was treated as the place of actual realization because the capacities [of sentient beings] were not yet mature.

Thus, through the three cycles of teaching, roots were first established and obstacles overcome, allowing them to become bodhisattvas before the truth of "long-term realization" was finally proclaimed.

Consequently, the increase of the Path and the reduction of births, the advancement to the stage of the "Successor," and the demonstration of extinction beneath the twin trees—these were all like a physician pointing out [the cure].
Nirvāṇa is fundamentally the manifestation of extinction as birth; therefore, by mentioning the intermediate state, one points back to the original extinction.
When Jñānaskandha initiated Mañjuśrī’s transformative activity, he proclaimed his departure with a hidden intent (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) to await conditions for remaining.

How could it be that the attendants of an ancient Buddha did not know Mañjuśrī was due to arrive, or that they were unaware the original sutra had not yet concluded, such that they would proclaim his departure while he remained? If one considers this...

Regarding the request to reassign [the classification]: because the *Nirdeśa-parivarta* (or the section on receiving and retaining) was judged to belong to the *Pravartana* (circulation), it must instead be assigned to the *Saddharma* (the True Dharma).
Because Master Fahui classified half a chapter of the "Treasure Stupa" (*Ratnakoṭi*) as belonging to the *Pravartana*, he caused the sutra to be fragmented.

Since the ancient masters judged that there are three aspects each for the *Hon* (Original) and *Jaku* (Trace), the principles of *Hon-jaku* are clearly manifest and the three meanings are further elucidated. Thus, one should know that assigning the *Pravartana* to the *Saddharma* is an error, and such a slight mistake is grave indeed.
This precisely belongs to the dissemination [of the teaching] which fails to benefit those of unsuitable capacity.
Question: When the Sūtra says, "At that time, the Buddha spoke these words of true and sincere reality," what is the meaning of this? Answer: This chapter has three parts:
first, Śākyamuni’s three exhortations; second, Maitreya’s four requests; and third, the Tathāgata’s formal instruction. This is the initial passage.
The wondrous essence of the three bodies resides at the ultimate limit of fruition; even those of superior wisdom cannot conceive of it, so how could those of inferior folly understand it?

Fearing that their minds might harbor doubts and their mouths commit slander, thereby causing injury to the Dharma, I have issued these three earnest exhortations before presenting this correct exposition.

Yet, fearing further that their ears may not be single-minded toward the Dharma teachings and their minds do not look up toward the sublime source, and that sentient beings are dull by nature when they hear...

Unable to understand it so that the Dharma might enter their hearts, [the Buddha] instructed and manifested the three bodies (trikāya) two or three times. Now, if this were merely for the sake of circulation, it would apply only to the preceding Dharma;
yet the preceding Dharma is but the One Vehicle (ekayāna), wherein provisional and ultimate truths are unified—why then is there a need for these three repeated exhortations?

Previously, when the Śrāvakas sought [to hear the teaching], it was judged to belong to the "Correct" (zheng) category; how much more so now, as this concerns Bodhisattvas, where it must belong to the "Circulation" (liutong) category, especially since the preceding request was already made?

However, these three [sections] extend through to the fourth; while the first is strictly for the sake of circulation, it remains uncertain whether the Three Bodies (*trikāya*) and the aforementioned One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) are identical or different.
If they are identical, then since this has already been heard, why is it that those of superior wisdom cannot fathom it?
They receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, yet they themselves do not know what these Three Bodies are that they cannot fathom. If one says they are different, for what reason...

Previously, you were commanded to enter the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) in which the three bodies (*trikāya*) do not exist. If there is no "one" apart from the three, how does this differ from the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*)?
If you say that the dharmas of the fruit cannot be fathomed by those below, and that only Buddha can know Buddha, then how could those below possibly fathom it?

Since you have already established this previously, why must you now claim that [the truth] exists only in the state of fruition? Thus, we know that you have not yet attained realization; you remain in the depths of ignorance, still slandering and still doubting, which is truly lamentable.

Since even disparaging [the teaching] does not qualify one as having attained the One Vehicle, how much less so for those who have not heard it with their ears and have lost the profound mystery of the mind?
Those of dull nature who have not heard the True Dharma remain entirely within the state of ordinary beings; thus, to claim they have received a prediction of enlightenment would be a falsehood.

Therefore, the intent behind the discourse on the Three Bodies lies in the distant future. People do not understand this and recklessly compose inquiries and chapters; hence we know that prior to this, the Three Bodies had already been explained. I have received [this teaching].
Those who are already established should certainly not depend on three proclamations; who would not know that the Buddha’s *gayāśīrṣa* [enlightenment] was first achieved?

How could there be a need for three cycles of teaching for one of superior wisdom destined for succession, yet for those of inferior dullness, it is only upon hearing this chapter that they realize the three bodies are fully present?

Thus we know that while those who receive the prediction after three cycles may achieve perfection in two more lifetimes, they still fear the arising of doubt. If even hearing this chapter might lead to injury or disparagement, for whom was this sutra spoken, and who is to be benefited? How much more so...

The delusions of doubt and slander, as well as the transgressions of injury and destruction, have already been eliminated at the stage of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*); these have long since been exhausted even prior to the Vaipulya (*vaipulya*) teachings.

How could it be that they are only truly resolved during the "Circulation Section" (*parīndanā*)? Furthermore, if this were necessarily part of the Circulation Section, why would it say, "Now for the first time, the correct teaching is set forth"?

Since the request for the correct teaching implies that the teaching has not yet been delivered, it cannot be considered the Circulation Section. Thus, the words of the Honored Master [Xuanzang] are not limited to this point alone; one knows that the recent interpretations are without merit.

One may rely upon this to understand that the three proclamations and four requests were made with sincere and earnest intent; that a single generation was uniquely singled out for these words has its basis. Question:
The sutra states, "At that time, the various bodhisattvas [requested] until the Buddha spoke. What is the meaning of this? Answer: This refers to the text of the four requests.
Since the Buddha, out of compassion, had already proclaimed to the great assembly three times, how could it have been in vain? Therefore, the four requests were added to manifest their longing.

Because the mind of the Dharma is held in high esteem, three proclamations were made to expound upon the three bodies (*trikāya*), each praying for the four virtues and longing for the four wisdoms to deliver the four classes of beings.
Now it is said that to repay the Buddha’s compassion, these three proclamations to the great assembly must not be in vain;

they appear like a reciprocal exchange of human affairs, merely responding to the expectations of the four seas. Thus, at this point, the frequent requests for instruction are like a person seeking goods—seeking them with earnest intent.

If "frequent" (*pin*) necessarily implies that things are precious, and "entrusted" (*zhuchong*) necessarily implies that things are rare, then how does this differ from what was stated previously regarding the four wisdoms and three bodies?

Furthermore, if it only benefits the four types of birth, it would not encompass those in the formless realm; it would thus permanently contradict the principle of transformation and deviate from the possibility of attaining the cessation of birth.
Question: What is the meaning of the passage in the Sūtra from "At that time" through "the power"? Answer: This is the Tathāgata’s direct teaching. Regarding the term "secret" (*guhya*):

it refers to the two bodies of Dharma and Reward (*dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*). Regarding "supernatural power" (*abhijñā*): it refers to the Buddha of Transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*). That which is concealed and protected is called "secret"; that which is profound and difficult to understand is called "mysterious" (*guhya*).
Now, it is said that the previously explained True Aspect (*tathatā*) and One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) are the provisional and real [teachings] of all Buddhas.
If wisdom has not yet engaged with that which is led by the three cycles of the secrets of the three bodies (*trikāya*), how could it be otherwise?
If one does not realize the three bodies, one remains the same as those of the Hīnayāna; since the five parts [of the path] were already attained previously, what need is there for the three cycles?

Furthermore, the faith regarding these secrets was never mentioned prior to this, and it is still protected even now; is this not a mistaken interpretation? Therefore, at the beginning of the "Expedient Means" chapter, the true reality of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is precisely...

The Dharma-body is that which the Buddha has accomplished, which is precisely the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*); terms such as "expedient means" refer to the Responsive and Transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Therefore, one should know that prior to this, he had already heard of the Responsive body at Gayā;

since there must necessarily be a Dharma-body corresponding to that Responsive body, it is for a profound reason that he now earnestly requests the teaching of the long-distant Dharma and Reward-bodies through the medium of the present Responsive body. That master further cites the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*:
Among these, there are four types of secrecy; those secrets of the Buddha within the Vaipulya [sūtras] should all be definitively understood. As for what are called the "four":
first is the secret of causing entry, which means teaching form as conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) to śrāvakas so that they may be free from fear and gradually enter the holy teaching.
It is not that everything exists; rather, this is a provisional teaching (*upāya-deśanā*) regarding existence, which conceals the reality—this is the secret. Second...

Regarding the "secrecy of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-guhya*): this refers to teaching that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), unarisen, and unceasing based upon the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
By thus refuting the perceived characteristics of existence, they are described as being non-existent.

Now, since this "non-existence" is a negation of grasping and still employs the provisional (*upāya*) to conceal the ultimate reality, one knows that in the true principle, the three natures are simultaneous; they are neither arising nor ceasing, and should not be categorized as either existent or non-existent.

Third, regarding the secret of counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa-guhya*), the Buddha teaches various doctrines in order to eliminate various obstacles; specifically, to remove eight types of obstacles:

first, to remove the obstacle of disparaging the Buddha; second, to remove the obstacle of disparaging the Dharma, he says, "I was formerly named Vipaśyin," because the *dharmakāya* is identical [in all Buddhas];
third, to remove laziness, as when it is said that those who vow to be born in Sukhāvatī will all attain rebirth there, and so forth; fourth, to remove...
1. To eliminate the obstacle of being easily satisfied with minor virtues: one either praises or disparages a single root of virtue. 2. To eliminate the obstacle of craving for sensory pleasures:
one praises the wealth, happiness, and magnificent adornments of the pure lands. 3. To eliminate the obstacle of pride: one praises the various Buddhas as having superior qualities. 4.

To eliminate the obstacle of regret that hinders the cultivation of virtue: one explains that although others may slight or disparage me, those sentient beings will nonetheless be reborn in the celestial realms.
The eighth [purpose] is to eliminate the obstacle of indeterminate nature, causing [beings] to abandon the inferior aspirations of the śrāvakas and recording that they shall become Buddhas;
furthermore, it is said that there is but one vehicle (ekayāna) and no second. Now, among these eight, the first seven are still characterized by diversity;
because they have not yet realized the single reality, the provisional covers the real and is thus termed "esoteric. Therefore, the teaching that śrāvakas become Buddhas is expounded last.

Because it was previously unbearable, it is called "secret"; by this standard, one should know that even those whose śrāvaka faculties have degenerated can still attain Buddhahood, let alone others who possess wholesome roots.
Furthermore, among the remaining seven types [of secrets], all are provisional antidotes;

therefore, one cannot use the term "equality" to prove the present teaching, for the text of this sutra consists entirely of definitive (real) discourse. Fourth, the secret of transformation, as in the teaching on awakening.
That which is not firm is made firm; one who dwells well within inversion and is afflicted by extreme afflictions attains supreme enlightenment.
It is said that its true essence is obtained only at a later time; this is a cryptic teaching regarding the "later time," and thus it is called a secret discourse (*guhyatantra*).
Such secret terminology should be understood as being distinct from this [ordinary] context. Herein, "secret" refers to the third [category], because of its lightness.
Regarding those who, out of greed and pride for the Buddha’s virtues, claim that the bodies of other Buddhas are their own and thus praise the Buddha—as stated in the passage below:

"In the interval between these [lifetimes], I spoke of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and others"—if one says this refers to the Śrāvakas belonging to the first three cycles (*triparivarta*), then since the remaining text does not even accord with the intent of the first three cycles, how much less so this particular passage? As for citing this as scriptural evidence, it has already been refuted previously.
Having finished the explanation, why was it necessary to state it with such earnestness three times and request it four times? Was it for fear that [the audience] would not believe?

Therefore, we know that prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, Śākyamuni had already attained Buddhahood; thus, one must not interpret everything as having an "equal intention" (*samaprābhisaṃdhi*), because this teaching of his long-attained Buddhahood belongs to the category of "facts" (*vastu*). Even if one points to the Buddha-body (*buddhakāya*) as being equal, it is likewise [not the case].
Regarding the term "not yet perfected" and so forth, one must say that only when mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated can it be called equality;

thus we know that the *Ratnagotravibhāga*’s description of the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is not the reward body of long duration. If other sutras still lack this [teaching], how much more so the case of that treatise?
Question: The Sūtra states, "All the world up to the attainment of *sambodhi*. What does this mean? Answer: This is the formal exposition of the lifespan;
why then do you ask about the beginning of the dissemination? Furthermore, according to the Śāstra, this section consists of only two parts:

the first clarifies that there is no higher than *bodhi*, and from the words "Good sons" onwards, it reiterates the manifestation of the two bodies—the *vipāka-kāya* (retribution body) and the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (transformation body)—in terms of the accomplished lifespan.

Regarding the characteristics of their distinctions, the supreme *nirvāṇa* is presented in the initial passage through a threefold division that demonstrates the *bodhi* of the three types of Buddhas:
First is the *bodhi* of the *nirmāṇakāya* (Transformation Buddha), which manifests according to the perceptions of those who behold it. As the sutra states:
"All say that the Tathāgata departed from the palace of the Śākya clan, went not far from the city of Gayā, and sat at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to attain *samyaksambodhi*."
Second is the *vipākabuddha* (Reward Buddha) Bodhi: the fulfillment of the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and the eternal bliss of *nirvāṇa*, as the Sūtra says:
"Good son, since I truly attained Buddhahood, immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayuta* kalpas have passed. Third is the *dharmabuddha* (Dharma Buddha) Bodhi:
the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is the pure *nirvāṇa* that is eternally constant, pure, and unchanging, as the Sūtra says: [and so forth].

The Tathāgata knows and perceives the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are; because he does not perceive the triple world in the manner of those within the triple world, for what reason?
[The following passage] clarifies that the person who does not see is specifically referred to as the "Three Bodies" (*trikāya*).
Since the meaning of the Three Bodies applies generally while its specific intent here is particular, the scripture is cited stating "immeasurable."
Because it is boundless and so forth, it does not merely point to a long duration; rather, when speaking of the three bodies, it refers to the three bodies of the ancient teachings.

Since people were deluded regarding that long duration, it was judged to belong to the "circulation" category among the various sutras. But since this has not yet been discussed, how can one know it is eternally distinct?

The meaning of the treatise is most subtle; commentators themselves are confused about why Nirvana is supreme. It must be pointed out that the three virtues exist beyond the state of quiescent extinction, being fundamentally perfect, eternal, and constant throughout the long duration.
